abstract: |
 Automated vision models turn video into dense time series of emotion scores. Real score series alone cannot show whether a method for estimating dimensions would find the right structure if that structure were actually present. We introduce the Latent Oscillator Measurement Model (LOMM), a simulation framework with three layers that can be varied independently: latent dynamics, time-varying expression, and a measurement model that turns latent states into observed scores. LOMM generates either bounded scores that sum to one, like classifier probabilities, or continuous indicators with a known factor structure. Study 1 compared simulated with real score series from 100 MAFW video clips using five-fold cross-validation. Letting video clips differ in baseline score level and overall scale reduced the mean discrepancy from 0.3250 to 0.2567, a 21.0% improvement. Study 2 tested how well four methods recover the number of dimensions from continuous data with a known factor structure. With Louvain community detection, 100 observations per clip, and failed or timed-out fits counted as incorrect, accuracy was 0.939 for DynEGA, 0.884 for static EGA, 0.777 for GraphicalVAR, 0.176 for GIMME, and 1.000 for an oracle given the true structure. A population analysis shows that networks built from derivatives and networks built from lagged residuals share the same $1/(k-1)$ upper bound on within-dimension partial correlations, so using derivatives carries no automatic advantage. Shorter time series and independent starting states reduced accuracy, whereas gradual rather than abrupt changes in expression mattered little. The two studies answer different questions, and Study 2 does not establish recovery from bounded scores. LOMM lets researchers test dynamic methods against a known structure before treating patterns in classifier scores as substantive findings.

# Introduction

Video is increasingly used as a source of intensive behavioral data because it preserves the temporal ordering of visible action and can be analyzed at a resolution that manual frame-by-frame coding cannot sustain. Deep-learning systems can now convert frames or short video segments into dense time series of model-derived emotional-expression scores [@meng2017IdentityAware; @li2022Deep]. In a facial-expression recognition task, a model maps each image or segment to category probabilities or continuous scores for labels such as happiness, anger, sadness, fear, surprise, disgust, or neutral expression.

These score streams are valuable because many behavioral questions concern how visible affect unfolds over time. Researchers may ask whether expressive states persist or switch, whether they return after perturbation, and whether many model-output channels reflect a smaller number of expressive dimensions. Such questions arise in psychotherapy, autism assessment, collaborative work, public communication, and social-media video [@halamovaAutomatedFacialExpression2023; @holidayMultimodalEmotionPerspective2023; @liDecodingGroupEmotional2024; @manelisbaramComparingThreeAlgorithms2025].

Automated facial-analysis systems now make this kind of work feasible at scale. Datasets such as FER2013 supported deep-learning approaches to facial-expression recognition, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [@goodfellow2013Challenges; @arriaga2017Realtimea; @ezerceli2022Convolutional]. Most early systems inherited emotion categories from their training data and returned scores for fixed labels such as anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise, and neutral facial expression [@wang2022Rethinking]. CLIP-based and related vision-language models also support zero-shot classification with user-specified labels [@radford2021LearningTransferable; @foteinopoulou2023EmoCLIP; @li2023CLIPER; @tomasevic2026TransforEmotion]. Each frame can therefore be represented by a vector of prompt-defined classifier scores.

Facial-expression benchmarks also show why these scores require task-specific validation. FER-adapted vision-language models such as CLIPER and EmoCLIP improve on an unadapted CLIP baseline by adding expression-specific text descriptions or training objectives [@li2023CLIPER; @foteinopoulou2023EmoCLIP]. EmoCLIP, for example, reported gains exceeding 10 percentage points in weighted average recall and 5 points in unweighted average recall over CLIP on several zero-shot video benchmarks. Such gains indicate that performance depends on model adaptation, the label set, prompt construction, and the evaluation dataset. These accuracy studies do not establish calibration of arbitrary prompt-defined scores, and the eleven-channel scoring procedure examined here has no frame-level label-validity claim.

The central obstacle is measurement. Emotional-expression scores are trained-model outputs that index visible behavior through a scoring procedure. Facial-expression technologies may be used for emotion recognition or for social-interaction analysis, and these interpretations answer different questions [@mckeownAreFacialExpression2024]. A further psychometric question is whether multiple score channels should be analyzed separately or treated as fallible indicators of lower-dimensional expressive processes [@russellCoreAffect2003; @mehu2015Emotion; @nesselroade2002]. Measurement error can alter the structure recovered by dynamic methods [@kankaanpaa2026multipleindicator]. Method evaluation must therefore separate latent temporal organization from the process that turns it into observed scores.

This requirement raises a practical question that empirical data cannot answer: would a recovery method find the intended structure if it were present? Answering it requires a generator in which both latent dynamics and the multichannel observation process are known before estimation. Oscillator models provide parameters for level, velocity, feedback, and perturbation in intraindividual dynamics [@boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @ollero2023Characterizing]. A useful validation design must also vary dimensionality, indicator blocks, measurement quality, and activity while preserving a known recovery target.

This paper introduces the Latent Oscillator Measurement Model (LOMM), a simulation tool that generates emotional-expression score series whose structure is known in advance. LOMM separates three operations. A latent layer generates the underlying trajectories, an activity layer controls which dimensions are expressed at each moment, and an observation layer turns those trajectories into noisy scores on many channels. Researchers can specify the number of latent dimensions, the dynamic parameters, loading strength, measurement error, the activity pattern, how much video clips differ from one another, and whether the simulated scores are bounded or continuous. All of these are fixed before any method is applied, so what a method recovers can be compared with what generated the data.

LOMM integrates established modeling ideas in a single generative design. Differential-equation models represent level and velocity, continuous-time state-space models motivate the exact transition between observation times, and dynamic factor models motivate the multivariate measurement structure [@boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @nesselroade2002; @nesselroade2008dfm]. The contribution lies in their measurement-first integration: latent dynamics, activity, and observation geometry can be varied independently while the indicator partition remains known.

We use this framework in two linked studies. Study 1 asks whether simulated score series reproduce the statistical properties of real classifier scores from 100 MAFW video clips, evaluated with five-fold cross-validation. Study 2 asks whether four methods recover the correct number of dimensions, and the correct assignment of variables to dimensions, from simulated continuous data with a known factor structure. A follow-up sensitivity analysis tests whether recovery changes when video clips differ in their baseline score levels and overall variability.

A population-level analysis compares the networks these methods estimate on a common scale. When all loadings are equal, the derivative-based network estimated by DynEGA and the lagged-residual network estimated by GraphicalVAR approach the same upper bound on within-dimension partial correlations, $1/(k-1)$ for $k$ indicators per dimension. Which method does better therefore depends on the signal-to-noise ratio and the length of the time series, not on whether a network is built from derivatives or from lagged residuals.

## Present Research

Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis [DynEGA; @golino2020modeling] is the focal method because it was designed to find groups of variables whose changes are coordinated over time. GraphicalVAR and GIMME are neighboring methods for intensive longitudinal data; each estimates a different structure and turns it into a network in a different way. Static EGA, which ignores the time ordering entirely, shows how much can be recovered from score levels alone. Finally, an oracle receives the true structure and passes it through the same community-detection step as the other methods, which checks that the shared machinery works as intended.

The paper addresses three questions. First, how closely do simulated score series reproduce the statistical properties of real classifier scores, judged on video clips held out from calibration? Second, how well do DynEGA, static EGA, GraphicalVAR, and GIMME recover a known factor structure from simulated continuous data? Third, how does that recovery change under shorter time series, independent starting states, gradual rather than abrupt changes in expression, cross-loadings, correlated residuals within a dimension, correlated inputs across dimensions, and bounded scores? The oracle answers none of these questions on its own; it is an implementation check rather than a target that a real estimator could be expected to reach.

The two studies answer different questions and support different conclusions. Study 1 asks only whether simulated data resemble real data on a set of chosen summary statistics; it says nothing about whether any structure can be recovered. Study 2 asks only whether methods recover a structure we planted; it says nothing about whether the simulated data look like real classifier output. The sensitivity analysis sits inside Study 2: it adds between-clip differences in baseline and scale while keeping the data-generating factor structure fixed. @fig-pipeline shows how the two studies relate.

Appendix B gives the population-level argument behind Study 2. Under ideal measurement, indicators belonging to the same dimension share a common signal, and indicators belonging to different dimensions are uncorrelated in the population. Weaker loadings, larger measurement error, less expressive activity, and dependence across dimensions all shrink the separation a method has to work with. The simulations then test departures from that ideal, and they always distinguish whether a method produced a usable result at all from how accurate it was when it did.

## The Latent Oscillator Measurement Model

LOMM starts from a measurement problem. A video yields one score per emotion label per frame, and the simulation treats those scores as fallible indicators of a smaller number of underlying expressive processes. Over a short clip, expression may stay low, rise briefly and subside, persist, or alternate between states. A useful latent representation therefore has to describe a current level, a rate of change, a pull back toward rest, overshoot, damping, and random perturbation, all of which are central to research on affective dynamics [@kuppensEmotionDynamics2017; @houbenRelationShorttermEmotion2015; @hollensteinStateSpaceGrids2007].

Oscillator models describe exactly these features. Prior work has used them for intraindividual dynamics in which a current level and its rate of change jointly determine what happens next [@boker2002Method; @boker2015Adaptive; @ollero2023Characterizing]. LOMM builds on that representation and adds two further layers, giving the three introduced above: latent, activity, and observation. The observation layer produces either bounded scores that sum to one or continuous indicators with a known factor structure [@nesselroade2002; @golino2020modeling]. The three layers can be varied independently, which is what allows a simulated dataset to be attributed to a specific part of the generating process. This section describes each layer with the minimum notation needed to follow the studies; Appendix A gives the complete formal specification.

The latent layer treats each expressive dimension as a damped oscillator observed at equally spaced times. Let $n=1,\ldots,T$ index observations, let $\Delta>0$ be the interval between them, and define physical time as $t_n=(n-1)\Delta$. Video $i$ and dimension $f$ have a state $\mathbf{s}_{if,n}=[x_{if,n},v_{if,n}]^\top$ holding the current level and its rate of change. The state moves forward one step according to

\begin{equation}
\mathbf{s}_{if,n+1}
=
\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)\mathbf{s}_{if,n}
+
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)q_{if,n},
\qquad
q_{if,n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{qf}^{2}).
\label{eq:lomm-latent}
\end{equation}

Two parameters govern each dimension, and they are collected in the feedback matrix

$$
\mathbf{A}_f=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
\eta_f & \zeta_f
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Position feedback $\eta_f$ sets how strongly the process is pulled back toward its resting level, and velocity feedback $\zeta_f$ sets how quickly movement is damped. Together they determine the natural period of an oscillation and how fast an expressive episode fades. The matrix $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)=\exp(\mathbf{A}_f\Delta)$ carries the state forward deterministically across one observation interval, and the vector $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)$ distributes the random acceleration input $q_{if,n}$ across the level and its rate of change. Because these two quantities are computed exactly rather than approximated by a discretization, simulated trajectories are correct at any observation interval $\Delta$. Appendix A gives their closed forms.

The acceleration inputs are what keep a trajectory from settling into a smooth decay: they perturb the process at every step, producing the continuing peaks, reversals, and irregular movement visible in real expression. Their standard deviation is $\sigma_{qf}$. They are independent across videos, dimensions, and time steps, and they are independent of initial states, activity schedules, and measurement error.

The sign of the two feedback parameters determines the regime. When both are negative, the dimension is stable: it oscillates and settles back toward its resting level. When velocity feedback is positive, movement is amplified instead, and the trajectory grows over the observed record. We include such conditions deliberately as stress tests rather than as plausible affective regimes, and we report a diagnostic for how large the resulting trajectories become (Appendix A gives the stability conditions and the amplification diagnostics; @tbl-scenario-families lists which scenarios use which regime).

Dimensions are uncoupled: $\eta_f$, $\zeta_f$, and $\sigma_{qf}$ may differ across dimensions, but no dimension drives another. Study 2's main conditions start every dimension of every video from the same state ($x_{if,1}=0.25$, $v_{if,1}=2$), and a sensitivity analysis instead draws starting states independently for each video and dimension. This distinction matters more than it might appear: a shared starting state creates a transient that every dimension has in common, which is itself recoverable structure. Appendix A gives the stationary distribution used for the independent starts.

The activity layer decides which dimension is actually being expressed at each moment. It multiplies each latent trajectory by a nonnegative activity value, giving $\tilde{x}_{if,n}=a_{if,n}x_{if,n}$, and this product is what the observation layer sees. The activity values follow a scenario-specific schedule built from an active level, a low background level, and dwell times that determine how long each state lasts. In single-dominance scenarios, one dimension stays highly expressed for the whole clip. In switching scenarios, the expressed dimension changes after sampled dwell intervals. In low-expression scenarios, every dimension stays near the background level.

Whether activity changes abruptly or gradually is worth separating from the latent dynamics, because an abrupt switch is itself a large change in the observed series. A method that works with derivatives will see a spike at that switch even though the underlying oscillator did not accelerate. We therefore run a sensitivity analysis that replaces each abrupt switch with a five-observation gradual transition while holding the dimensions and their indicators fixed. Appendix A gives the exact identity separating the contribution of the changing activity from the contribution of the changing trajectory.

The observation layer turns the activity-scaled trajectories into observed scores. It does so in two steps: it first builds a vector of coordinates from the latent positions, and then places that vector on whichever scale the study requires. For video $i$ at observation $n$, the first step is

\begin{equation}
\mathbf u_{in}
=\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf b_i
+\kappa s_i\left(\boldsymbol\Lambda\tilde{\mathbf x}_{in}
+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{in}\right),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{in}\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_i).
\label{eq:lomm-measurement}
\end{equation}

This is an ordinary factor model with two additions. The familiar parts are the loading matrix $\boldsymbol\Lambda$, which maps the $m$ activity-scaled latent positions onto the observed coordinates, the measurement error $\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{in}$, and a fixed center $\boldsymbol\mu$ shared by all videos. The measurement errors are independent over time and across videos, and independent of everything in the latent and activity layers. The additions are the two video-specific terms that let clips differ from one another: the baseline $\mathbf b_i$ shifts a whole clip's scores up or down, and the scale $s_i>0$ stretches or compresses both its signal and its noise. A global scale $\kappa>0$ multiplies the same quantities for every clip.

These two terms are the switch between the studies. Study 2's main conditions turn them off, setting $\mathbf b_i=\mathbf 0$ and $s_i=1$ so that every video shares one measurement model and the factor structure is the only source of shared variance. Study 1 turns them on and estimates them from data: the baseline is drawn from a distribution whose covariance is estimated from training clips, and the scale is drawn as $s_i\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0.5,1.5)$, which averages one. The sensitivity analysis in Study 2 turns them on in a restricted way, drawing baselines that lie within the space spanned by the loadings so that between-clip differences stay consistent with the factor structure rather than adding a new source of variance. Appendix A gives all three constructions.

Study 1's calibrated settings are a natural period of 12 observations, a damping ratio of 0.5, $\kappa=1$, and a measurement-error standard deviation of 0.25 in the contrast coordinates. Expressed as feedback parameters, these give $\eta_f=-0.2742$ and $\zeta_f=-0.5236$, with an acceleration-input standard deviation of $\sigma_{qf}=0.5418$ after scaling the trajectories to unit variance. Study 1's selected configuration holds activity constant at one; a separate variant adds a brief three-observation transition.

The second step places the coordinates on the reported scale, and this is where the two studies diverge. Study 2 uses the coordinates directly as continuous indicators, so each of the $p=mk$ observed variables loads on exactly one dimension and carries its own measurement error. This is the standard continuous factor model that dimensionality methods are designed for, which is why it is the setting in which we ask whether they recover a known structure. Study 1 instead needs output that looks like a classifier's, so LOMM maps the coordinates onto $J$ strictly positive scores that sum to one:

\begin{equation}
\mathbf p_{in}
=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf V\mathbf u_{in}}{\tau}\right).
\label{eq:lomm-composition}
\end{equation}

The softmax function exponentiates its argument and divides by the total, which is how a classifier turns raw outputs into scores that sum to one. The fixed matrix $\mathbf V$ expands the $d=J-1$ coordinates of $\mathbf u_{in}$ into $J$ channels, and the temperature $\tau>0$ controls how sharply the scores concentrate on a single channel. The construction has a property we rely on: because the columns of $\mathbf V$ are orthonormal and sum to zero, the log-ratio coordinates of $\mathbf p_{in}$ recover $\mathbf u_{in}/\tau$ exactly. The only thing lost in the map is a level common to all channels, which no set of scores constrained to sum to one could reveal in any case. Appendix A gives the log-ratio definitions, the construction of $\mathbf V$, and the full identification argument.

Study 2's continuous indicators are generated before this map is applied. Each of the $p=mk$ indicators has one primary loading on its own dimension and its own measurement error. So that indicators within a dimension are not identical, loadings are perturbed by $\operatorname{Unif}(-0.15,0.15)$ and residual variances by $\operatorname{Unif}(-0.01,0.01)$; because the smallest nominal loading in the design is 0.40 and the smallest nominal residual standard deviation is 0.125, these perturbations leave every loading and variance positive.

Whichever scale is used, the simulated channels represent classifier output about visible expression and nothing more. LOMM tests whether methods recover a measurement process we specified in advance under controlled loading strength, measurement error, dynamic regime, activity pattern, and between-clip variability. Whether the emotion labels attached to those channels are valid, and whether they correspond to subjective emotional experience, are separate questions the simulation cannot address. A neutral channel can appear in real classifier output, but it is never assigned to a latent dimension here unless a scenario deliberately specifies one.

To make this concrete, a three-dimensional LOMM could stand for approach-affiliation, threat-defense, and orienting-novelty. Score channels for happiness, amusement, trust, or smiling would then be indicators of approach-affiliation; channels for anger, fear, disgust, contempt, or anxiety would be indicators of threat-defense; and channels for surprise, anticipation, confusion, or attention would be indicators of orienting-novelty. These labels are an example of how a researcher might set up a simulation, not validated affect categories in the real MAFW scores. The example draws on affect taxonomies that distinguish broad dimensions, discrete expression families, and opponent tendencies [@russellCircumplexModel1980; @russellCoreAffect2003; @russellMehrabianThreeFactor1977; @plutchikNatureEmotions2001], and it is consistent with facial-expression benchmarks that combine categorical expression labels with dimensional ratings [@mollahosseiniAffectNetDatabase2019; @kolliasABAW2023; @mehu2015Emotion]. A different taxonomy can be encoded by changing which channels belong to which dimension, leaving everything else about LOMM unchanged.

### What LOMM Can and Cannot Identify

Knowing the settings that generated a dataset is not the same as being able to recover them from data, and LOMM is a generator rather than a model to be fitted. Several of its quantities are not separately identifiable even in principle. Dimensions are recoverable only up to a relabeling. The size of a loading can always be traded against the scale of the latent trajectory it multiplies, so neither is pinned down without an explicit constraint, and activity gain and acceleration-input variance both feed latent amplitude in the same confounded way. The bounded map adds two more: shifting every channel's input by a common constant leaves the scores unchanged, and the temperature can be absorbed into the scale of the coordinates.

The sampling rate imposes one further limit. An oscillation faster than half the sampling rate is indistinguishable from a slower one, so the observation interval sets a ceiling on the frequencies that could ever be identified. Every oscillation used here falls below that ceiling with room to spare. Study 1 uses $\Delta=1$, giving the most restrictive bound of approximately 3.14 against a largest angular frequency of approximately 0.78; Study 2 uses $\Delta\in\{0.25,0.4\}$, giving bounds of approximately 12.57 and 7.85 against a largest angular frequency of approximately 1.04. Fitting LOMM to real data would require constraints on factor sign and scale, on the activity schedule, on the loading or input scale, on the temperature, and on the frequency range; Appendix A states each of these formally. The simulations reported here estimate none of these parameters. They ask only what methods recover from data whose structure we fixed in advance.

@fig-dlosim shows the same three-dimension example twice to make the role of the random acceleration inputs visible.

#| fig-alt: "Two line plots comparing three decaying oscillators without random inputs with the same oscillators driven by random inputs."
