@fig-dlosim isolates what the random acceleration inputs contribute. With the inputs fixed at zero, the three stable dimensions oscillate and decay toward a common resting level. Adding random inputs to the same transition produces the continuing peaks, reversals, and irregular movement that make real expression series look the way they do. The figure shows latent trajectories only; persistent differences in the level of observed scores enter later, through the center and the video-clip baseline in Equation 2.


# Method

The analyses follow the workflow in @fig-pipeline. @tbl-study-design summarizes what each analysis simulates, what it targets, and what may be concluded from it. Study 1 lets video clips differ in baseline and scale and produces bounded scores that sum to one, because that is what real classifier output looks like. Study 2 switches both off, so every clip shares one measurement model and the factor structure is the only source of shared variance. A sensitivity analysis then reintroduces between-clip differences in a restricted form. All three use the same LOMM machinery and differ only in what they license us to conclude.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-study-design
#| tbl-cap: "What each analysis simulates and what it supports. Study 1 asks whether simulated data resemble real data; Study 2 asks whether methods recover a structure specified in advance."
#| results: asis

study_design_table <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Analysis, ~`Data type and configuration`, ~Target, ~Methods, ~`What it supports`,
  "Study 1: five-fold comparison", "Bounded scores summing to one; clips differ in baseline and scale", "Chosen summary statistics of real score series", "Comparison of eight configurations", "Similarity to real data in this sample",
  "Study 2: main benchmark ($T=100$)", "Continuous indicators; all clips share one measurement model", "Number of dimensions and assignment of variables to them", "DynEGA, static EGA, GraphicalVAR, GIMME, oracle", "Recovery under the data-generating factor structure",
  "Study 2: shorter series ($T=25$)", "Continuous indicators; all clips share one measurement model", "Number of dimensions and assignment of variables to them", "DynEGA, static EGA, GraphicalVAR, GIMME, oracle", "Recovery when each clip has fewer observations",
  "Study 2: targeted departures", "Continuous indicators; all clips share one measurement model", "Number of dimensions and assignment of variables to them", "DynEGA, static EGA, GraphicalVAR, oracle", "Sensitivity to starting states, activity transitions, loadings, residuals, and inputs",
  "Study 2: bounded-score departure", "Bounded scores summing to one, or their log-ratio coordinates", "Dimensions and variable assignment among the original channels", "DynEGA, static EGA, GraphicalVAR", "Recovery once scores are constrained to sum to one; the oracle is omitted because it never sees the transformed data",
  "Study 2: between-clip variability", "Continuous indicators; clips differ in baseline and scale within the loading space", "Number of dimensions and assignment of variables to them", "DynEGA, static EGA, GraphicalVAR, GIMME, oracle", "Whether recovery survives between-clip differences in selected conditions",
  "Study 2: broad grid", "Continuous indicators; all clips share one measurement model", "Number of dimensions and assignment of variables to them", "DynEGA", "DynEGA recovery across a wider range of conditions"
)
cat("\\begingroup\\tiny\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  study_design_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "p{1.32in}", "p{1.15in}", "p{1.35in}", "p{1.45in}")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

For one simulated video clip, the implementation draws a starting state and the random acceleration inputs, moves each dimension forward with Equation 1, applies the activity schedule, draws the clip baseline and scale, evaluates Equation 2, and finally returns either the continuous indicators or the bounded scores of Equation 3 together with their log-ratio coordinates. The R function `lomm_observe()` performs the observation step and records which configuration was used, the random-number seeds, and the loading and covariance matrices in effect. A runnable example and the exact configuration behind the figures in this paper accompany the analysis code.

## Study 1: Comparing Simulated and Real Score Series

@fig-mafwvideo illustrates the kind of real score series Study 1 compares against. MAFW, introduced as *MAFW: A Large-scale, Multi-modal, Compound Affective Database for Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition in the Wild*, supplies naturalistic video clips [@liu_mafw_2022]. The dataset does not validate the emotion labels, the scoring model, or the subjective emotional states of the people in the clips. Panel A reproduces four frames solely to clarify the academic analysis, following the small-portion publication allowance in the MAFW Academic User Agreement.^[MAFW Academic User Agreement, accessed August 13, 2026: \url{https://mafw-database.github.io/MAFW/academics/mafw-academics-final.pdf}.] No raw video is redistributed. Study 1 uses 100 video clips scored with the same zero-shot procedure as the illustration.

We used the transforEmotion R package to generate a score for each emotion label in each frame [@tomasevic2026TransforEmotion]. The retained scores identify the `oai-large` model setting, which denotes the OpenAI CLIP ViT-Large/14 model family. The scoring procedure sampled up to 50 frames uniformly from each video. A Haar cascade detected faces in each frame, and the largest detected face was expanded by 50 pixels on each side before classification; frames without a detected face received missing scores. Eleven raw lowercase class labels---anger, disgust, fear, happiness, neutral, sadness, surprise, contempt, anxiety, helplessness, and disappointment---were passed directly to the text encoder, without a sentence template. These channels follow the MAFW single-label schema and remain model outputs rather than frame-level human annotations. Burned-in subtitles were not explicitly masked. Subtitle pixels could therefore contribute only when they fell inside the padded face crop. Observed scores were required to lie in $[0,1]$; complete rows were retained only when their sum was positive, finite, and within $10^{-6}$ of one, then divided by that sum in the fixed component order. Values were not truncated, and zero replacement was disabled. The scoring-time package release and exact model-checkpoint revision were not archived, so exact frame rescoring cannot be guaranteed. The retained scores support all preprocessing and comparison analyses reported here. The main analysis kept only complete rows. A sensitivity analysis interpolated across internal gaps of at most two frames within a segment.

The four frames in Panel A come from one MAFW clip. Their scores differ across the channels labeled helplessness, fear, disgust, sadness, anxiety, and disappointment (Panel B), and the frame-by-frame trajectories change in bursts with irregular local movement (Panel C). Applying DynEGA to that single clip's non-neutral trajectories groups the channels into a network (Panel D). This last panel is an illustration of what these methods produce on real data, not evidence about what they recover; Study 2 addresses recovery using data whose structure is known.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mafwvideo
#| fig-cap: "Score series from one MAFW video clip. Panel A shows four frames reproduced to clarify the academic analysis under the MAFW research-use terms. Panel B shows the emotion scores assigned to those frames; Panel C shows smoothed trajectories for the channels with the highest mean scores; Panel D shows a DynEGA network estimated from the same clip's non-neutral trajectories. Scores were generated with transforEmotion using OpenAI CLIP ViT-Large/14."
#| fig-alt: "Four-panel illustration with selected video frames, their emotion scores, score trajectories over time, and a DynEGA network."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

figure_2_path <- file.path("figures", "mafw_video_dynega_example.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_2_path)) {
  figure_2_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "mafw_video_dynega_example.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_2_path)
```

The sample was assembled one video clip at a time, with MAFW category labels used to diversify it rather than as validation targets. The main analysis contains 3,557 frames in 188 clip segments; usable segment lengths range from 16 to 50 frames, with a median of 35. The gap-interpolated sensitivity analysis contains 3,632 frames in 129 segments, with lengths from 17 to 50 frames and a median of 36.5. Both retain 100 video clips spanning the 11 single-label categories. Because the segments are short, autocorrelation and spectral summaries should be read with caution.

We compare simulated with real data on eight summary statistics. Six describe a single channel over time: the median level, the interquartile range of the level, the interquartile range of frame-to-frame changes, the lag-1 autocorrelation, the entropy of monotonic run lengths, and the normalized spectral entropy. Two describe all channels together: effective rank and total variance. Each statistic is computed twice, once on the scores themselves and once on their log-ratio coordinates, giving 16 comparisons in total. For each comparison, we take the larger of two distances between the real and simulated distributions of that statistic across clips: the absolute difference in medians and the one-dimensional Wasserstein distance, both divided by a measure of how spread out the real values are. That divisor is the interquartile range where available, falling back in order to $1.4826\times\mathrm{MAD}$, the standard deviation, and one. Scores and log-ratio coordinates receive equal weight in the total, which we call the discrepancy. Smaller values mean the simulated data resemble the real data more closely on these particular statistics.

Video clips were split into five folds, assigned deterministically within MAFW category and length order, leaving 20 clips in each test fold. Everything about a fold's measurement model was estimated from its training clips only, so no test clip influenced the simulation it was later compared against. The center of the coordinate space was the mean of the training observations. After subtracting each clip's own mean, we kept the first three eigenvectors of the within-clip covariance, oriented each so that its largest coefficient was positive, and rescaled it by the square root of its eigenvalue divided by the root mean of the three retained eigenvalues. The covariance of the clip baselines was estimated from how far each training clip's mean fell from the overall mean, shrunk halfway toward its diagonal, with eigenvalues floored at $10^{-8}$ for numerical stability.

Within each fold and each configuration, we searched 27 candidate settings, crossing natural periods $\{8,12,24\}$, damping ratios $\{0.05,0.20,0.50\}$, and observation scales $\kappa\in\{0.75,1.00,1.25\}$, evaluating each on three paired training datasets. Selection averaged the eight discrepancies within each representation and weighted the two representations equally, breaking ties by the smaller worst-case discrepancy, then an observation scale closer to one, then stronger damping, then candidate order. All five folds selected the same settings for the configuration with both a clip baseline and a clip scale: a 12-observation period, a damping ratio of 0.50, and $\kappa=1$. The tolerance below which the scaling divisor fell back to the next option was $10^{-8}$.

Each selected configuration then generated 100 simulated datasets per test fold, matching the held-out clips' frame indices and segment structure so that the comparison is not confounded by differences in length or missingness. The discrepancy compares the distribution of each summary statistic across clips, not frame-by-frame values, since LOMM generates new realizations rather than reconstructing a particular video. The composite weights the two representations equally and averages the five folds. For uncertainty, we drew 2,000 bootstrap samples, resampling 20 clips with replacement within each fold and preserving the pairing across configurations, datasets, and statistics. The eight configurations are the factorial combinations of three components: an estimated clip baseline, a clip scale, and a brief activity transition.

## Choosing Simulation Scenarios

The scenarios connect Study 1 to Study 2, since both draw on the same latent and activity layers. Three sets of parameters define a scenario. The dynamic parameters are position feedback, velocity feedback, and acceleration-input variance ($\eta_f$, $\zeta_f$, and $\sigma_{qf}^2$). The activity parameters determine whether one dimension dominates throughout a clip, whether dominance switches after sampled dwell intervals, or whether all dimensions stay near a low background level. The measurement parameters are the loadings and residual covariances that turn latent trajectories into observed indicators.

The design contains six scenario families (@tbl-scenario-families). Four are stable, so trajectories oscillate and decay. The remaining two use positive velocity feedback so that trajectories grow over the record; these are stress tests rather than empirically calibrated affective regimes. Across families, the number of observed channels is $p=mk$, where $m$ is the number of dimensions and $k$ the number of indicators per dimension. Study 2's main benchmark uses $m\in\{2,3\}$, and the broad grid adds $m=4$. This range defines a deliberately low-dimensional recovery target; it is not an estimate of how many dimensions underlie real classifier scores, a question Study 1 addresses only indirectly through the effective-rank statistic.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scenario-families
#| tbl-cap: "The six scenario families. Dwell values are fractions of the time-series length; the codes label conditions in the results figures."
#| results: asis

scenario_family_table <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Code, ~Family, ~Switching, ~`Active/background gain`, ~`Dwell fraction`, ~`Dynamic rule`,
  "A", "Weak expression, one dominant dimension", "No", "0.35 / 0.05", "1.00 / 1.00", "Stable; low input scale",
  "B", "Strong expression, one dominant dimension", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Stable; standard input scale",
  "C", "Strong expression, switching dimension", "Yes", "1.00 / 0.08", "0.20 / 0.45", "Stable; standard input scale",
  "D", "Strong expression, rapid switching", "Yes", "1.25 / 0.08", "0.03 / 0.10", "Stable; high input scale",
  "E", "Growing trajectories, one dominant dimension", "No", "1.00 / 0.08", "1.00 / 1.00", "Positive velocity feedback; moderate input scale",
  "F", "Growing trajectories, switching dimension", "Yes", "1.10 / 0.10", "0.12 / 0.30", "Positive velocity feedback; higher input scale"
)
cat("\\begingroup\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  scenario_family_table,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("c", "l", "c", "c", "c", "l")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

Appendix F lists the exact feedback and acceleration-input values behind each family.

For each video, LOMM generates the latent trajectories, applies the activity schedule, and then constructs the observed data. Non-switching scenarios keep one dimension dominant for the whole clip and rotate which dimension that is across videos. Switching scenarios sample dwell intervals and change the dominant dimension over time. Study 1 uses bounded scores with a clip baseline and clip scale. Study 2 uses continuous indicators with uncorrelated measurement error and the small loading and variance perturbations described above.

## Study 2: Recovery of Dimensions from Data with Known Structure

Study 2 starts from a known answer: the number of dimensions and the assignment of each indicator to a dimension are both fixed before any data are generated. Its main conditions give every video clip the same measurement model, and the sensitivity analysis adds between-clip differences that stay within the space spanned by the loadings. Bounded scores are reserved for Study 1, because constraining scores to sum to one changes the associations among the original channels and therefore no longer preserves the structure we planted.

The four methods estimate different things, so they are compared at the one point where their outputs are commensurable: the grouping of variables. Each method receives the same simulated data, estimates its own structure, converts that structure into a network by a rule fixed in advance, and then passes the network to the same community-detection algorithm. What that algorithm returns is compared with the true assignment of variables to dimensions. The methods do not all use the same rows of data on the way there --- DynEGA loses rows to time-delay embedding, GraphicalVAR loses rows to forming lagged pairs --- and we deliberately do not force them onto a common subset, since each method's row handling is part of the method. Two things this comparison does not address: whether the emotion labels attached to real channels are valid, and which method is better for substantive emotion research.

We compare Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis [DynEGA; @golino2020modeling] with GraphicalVAR [@epskampggm; @graphicalVAR2024] and GIMME [@gates2012group; @lane2019uncovering] because they are neighboring approaches to structure in intensive longitudinal data. DynEGA is the focal method because it estimates groups of variables whose changes are coordinated over time, which is directly what Study 2 asks about. GraphicalVAR separates relations across consecutive time points from relations within the same time point; we group the variables using the latter. GIMME estimates a separate model for each video clip and we aggregate the resulting structures before grouping, which places it under more strain than the other methods and makes it as much a test of feasibility as of accuracy. Treating clips as separate series in this way is not how GIMME is normally used, and our results should not be read as evidence about its performance in person-level idiographic modeling.

DynEGA combines time-delay embedding, derivative estimation, and exploratory graph analysis [@glla2010; @golino2017ega1; @golino2019investigating]. Each video is passed through the `id` argument so that embedding windows never span two clips. We selected the embedding dimension with an explicit loop that fit every admissible candidate and minimized the Total Entropy Fit Index [TEFI; @golino2019entropy], breaking ties in favor of the shorter embedding. For $T=100$ the candidates were $\{5,10,15,25,50\}$; for the shorter series we used $\{5,6,10,12\}$. Selected counts for $T=100$ were 141, 242, 7,206, 5,509, and 8,502, respectively; for $T=25$ they were 2,327, 2,735, 6,068, and 10,470. EGAnet 2.3.0 estimated first derivatives with `tau = 1`, a `delta = 1` observation interval, and `use.derivatives = 1`, retaining the default `corr = "auto"` and `na.data = "pairwise"` settings. Neither our code nor the executed package path added noise to zero-variance channels. Rescaling every derivative from observation units to physical-time units would multiply all channels by the same positive constant, leaving the correlation matrix unchanged. We set `model = "glasso"` to estimate a regularized partial-correlation network with EBICglasso. Before community detection, each fitted network was symmetrized and its negative edges set to zero, with absolute weights used only when no positive edge remained. The seed for each simulated dataset determines its random draws, and a deterministic method-specific offset initializes each fit. Louvain community detection at resolution 1.0 was the primary grouping algorithm [@blondel2008fast]; Leiden [@traag2019leiden] and Walktrap [@pons2006walktrap] were applied to the same fitted network as sensitivity analyses.

GraphicalVAR estimates a graphical vector autoregressive model for intensive longitudinal data [@epskampggm; @graphicalVAR2024]. It produces two networks: a temporal network of directed regressions from one time point to the next, and a contemporaneous network of partial correlations among residuals at the same time point, after the lagged effects have been accounted for. In multilevel applications it can further separate within-person from between-person structure. We fit it with `mlGraphicalVAR` to the stacked simulated data, with video identity as the grouping variable, within-clip centering (`centerWithin = TRUE`), variable standardization (`scale = TRUE`), and `gamma = 0.5`. Variables are standardized across the stacked data and then centered within clip before lagged pairs are formed, and those pairs never cross a clip boundary. We group the variables using the returned contemporaneous partial-correlation matrix `fixedPCC`, because Study 2 asks about an undirected grouping of channels rather than about directed effects. Its diagonal is ignored and the result is treated as an undirected weighted graph defined by positive edges, with absolute weights used only when no positive edge is available. Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap are applied to that same fitted structure.

GIMME is an automated time-series approach built on unified structural equation modeling and vector autoregression [@gates2012group; @lane2019uncovering]. Each video clip was supplied as one time series with standardized variables. We extracted the standardized residual covariance matrices returned in `fit$psi`, then averaged them over usable clips, symmetrized them, removed the diagonal, and set negative values to zero before community detection. The resulting graph is a residual-covariance graph, not a residual-correlation or partial-correlation graph: it keeps the magnitude of residual covariance as the edge weight, so unequal residual variances can influence the grouping. We therefore read GIMME's results as specific to this conversion. Variable names fixed the column order across clips. A matrix left with no positive edge yielded one community per variable rather than falling back to absolute weights. Louvain was primary; Leiden and Walktrap were applied to the same graph.

DynEGA, static EGA, GraphicalVAR, GIMME, and the oracle all receive the same simulated data and are judged against the same true grouping. GraphicalVAR and GIMME were left out of the broad 518,400-dataset extension because evaluating them across a complete factorial design was not computationally practical; both were included in the main benchmark, and GraphicalVAR was also included in the targeted departures and the between-clip-variability analysis. Appendix B places the networks these methods estimate on a common population scale.

The main $T=100$ design contains 21,600 simulated datasets: six scenario families, $m\in\{2,3\}$ dimensions, $N\in\{50,100\}$ videos, residual standard deviations of $\{0.125,0.25,0.50\}$, loadings of $\{0.40,0.60,0.80\}$, four indicators per dimension, and 100 paired replications. Every method received the same dataset within each condition and replication. Louvain at resolution 1.0 was the primary grouping algorithm, with Leiden and Walktrap as paired sensitivity analyses.

Static EGA applies EBICglasso and the same grouping step to each dataset's contemporaneous correlation matrix, ignoring the time ordering entirely. The oracle skips estimation and simply passes a graph containing the true within-dimension edges, and no others, through that same grouping step. It therefore verifies that the conversion, variable ordering, and scoring work correctly, and provides a ceiling that no method estimating from data could be expected to exceed.

Not every fit succeeds, and how failures are counted turns out to matter a great deal for the comparison. We therefore report three quantities. The first is the probability that a method returned a usable result at all, $P(\mathrm{usable})$. The second is the probability that it found the correct number of dimensions given that it did, $P(\widehat m=m\mid\mathrm{usable})$. The third combines them into the probability that a method both produced a usable result and got the number of dimensions right, $P(\mathrm{usable\ and\ correct})$. Because this last quantity counts every failure and timeout as an error, we call it *worst-case accuracy*, and it is the headline number throughout: a method that often fails to return anything is not useful even if it is accurate whenever it does.

Three further diagnostics describe the grouping itself, among usable fits only. The adjusted Rand index (ARI) and variation of information compare the estimated grouping with the true one. Assignment accuracy matches estimated groups to true dimensions optimally, counts every indicator in the denominator, and treats an indicator placed in an unmatched group as incorrect. We also compare recovered trajectories with the activity-scaled latent positions $\tilde x$ that actually entered the measurement model. Within each dataset, indicators are standardized and each estimated group is summarized by its first principal component, falling back to a row mean when that cannot be computed. Trajectory correlation pairs each true dimension with its highest absolute correlation among the estimated summaries, which neither penalizes extra groups nor requires one-to-one matching. NRMSE instead matches estimated with true trajectories one-to-one after sign alignment, assigning the prespecified penalty of 2 to any true dimension left unmatched while ignoring extra estimated groups. In the marginal summaries, unusable fits receive a correlation of 0 and an NRMSE of 2. None of these diagnostics replaces worst-case accuracy.

Errors and timeouts stay in the denominator of every worst-case rate. Because the three community-detection algorithms are applied to one fitted structure rather than to three separate fits, they are sensitivity analyses rather than independent observations, and the main text reports Louvain only. Uncertainty comes from 2,000 resamples of whole simulated datasets, stratified by condition, with Monte Carlo standard errors from delete-one-dataset jackknifing.

A second analysis repeated the same 21,600-dataset design with shorter time series ($T=25$, $\Delta=0.4$, spanning 9.6 units of physical time). A set of targeted departures then fixed $N=100$, $T=100$, a loading of 0.60, a residual standard deviation of 0.25, and four indicators per dimension, crossing the six scenario families, two dimensionalities, and 50 paired replications; @tbl-challenge-variants states exactly what each departure changes. The broad DynEGA extension crossed $N\in\{50,100\}$, $T\in\{100,300\}$, $m\in\{2,3,4\}$, $k\in\{4,6\}$, loadings of $\{0.40,0.60,0.80\}$, residual standard deviations of $\{0.125,0.25,0.50\}$, and the six scenarios, giving 1,296 conditions with 400 replications each (518,400 datasets). It used the EGA package's own rule for deciding whether a fitted network was unidimensional. Because $T=100$ and $T=300$ use $\Delta=0.4$ and $\Delta=0.25$ respectively while holding the per-step input variance fixed, the difference between them reflects both the number of observations and the interval between them, not length alone.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-challenge-variants
#| tbl-cap: "The targeted departures. Each row changes one element of the ideal condition, holding everything else fixed."
#| results: asis

challenge_variant_table <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Departure, ~Specification,
  "Independent starting states", "Each video and dimension starts independently: stationary zero-mean starts for stable dimensions, $x_0\\sim\\mathrm{Unif}(-0.25,0.25)$ and $v_0\\sim\\mathrm{Unif}(-2,2)$ for growing ones",
  "Gradual activity transitions", "A five-observation gradual transition replaces each abrupt switch",
  "Cross-loadings", "Each indicator gains small loadings on other dimensions: $N(0,0.05^2)$ additions truncated to $[-0.10,0.10]$",
  "Correlated residuals within a dimension", "Residual correlation of $0.10$ among the indicators of each dimension",
  "Correlated inputs across dimensions", "Acceleration-input correlation of $0.15$ between every pair of dimensions",
  "Bounded scores", "Scores mapped through the softmax with $\\tau=1$, analyzed either as scores or as log-ratio coordinates"
)
cat("\\begingroup\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{4pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  challenge_variant_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "p{4.8in}")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

## Computational Environment

Analyses used R 4.5.1 on Rocky Linux 8.8 (`x86_64-redhat-linux-gnu`) with dual Intel Xeon Silver 4310 processors, 48 logical threads, and 125 GiB RAM. Key package versions were EGAnet 2.3.0, graphicalVAR 0.3.4, gimme 10.0, igraph 2.2.1, qgraph 1.9.8, psych 2.5.6, lavaan 0.6-20, dplyr 1.1.4, and ggplot2 4.0.1. OpenBLAS 0.3.15 and LAPACK 3.9.0 supplied numerical linear algebra. Parallel analyses used one BLAS thread per worker. DynEGA used 16 workers on the broad grid and 32 for the matched-network partitions; GraphicalVAR and GIMME used 24 workers with a 900-second limit per structure fit.

Runtime is elapsed wall-clock time in seconds, recorded with `proc.time()[["elapsed"]]` for fits that succeeded. For GraphicalVAR and GIMME it includes both fitting the structure and converting it into a grouping. Because one fitted structure is reused for Louvain, Leiden, and Walktrap, we count fits and results separately: feasibility is reported per unique fit, whereas accuracy is reported per fit-and-algorithm combination. Runtime summaries use successful fits only, while timeouts and errors remain in the denominators for feasibility and accuracy. These runtimes describe what this workflow costs on this machine and should not be read as hardware-independent speed benchmarks for the underlying methods.

# Results

## Study 1 Results: Similarity of Simulated and Real Score Series

Study 1 asks whether simulated score series reproduce chosen statistical properties of real classifier scores from 100 MAFW video clips. We name the eight configurations by which components they include. In the *identical-clips* configuration, every video shares one measurement model. The *baseline-only* configuration lets clips differ in their overall score level. The *baseline-and-scale* configuration lets them differ in both level and variability. The remaining four configurations add a brief activity transition to each of these. @fig-empirical-realism reports the mean discrepancy for all eight, computed on held-out clips and shown separately for the scores themselves and for their log-ratio coordinates. Smaller values mean closer agreement.

```{r}
#| label: fig-empirical-realism
#| fig-cap: "Discrepancy between simulated and real score series for the eight configurations, averaged over five cross-validation folds. Points are means across the eight summary statistics within each representation; smaller values indicate closer agreement with the real scores from 100 MAFW video clips. The diamond marks the baseline-and-scale configuration. Bootstrap intervals are not shown for individual configurations because their distributions were strongly displaced from the estimates themselves; Appendix C reports those diagnostics."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot comparing the discrepancy between simulated and real data for eight configurations, on scores and on log-ratio coordinates."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.95\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_4_path <- file.path("figures", "compositional_profile_discrepancy.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_4_path)) {
  figure_4_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "compositional_profile_discrepancy.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_4_path)
```

Averaging over both representations, the baseline-and-scale configuration had a mean discrepancy of 0.2567, compared with 0.3250 for the identical-clips configuration, a reduction of 21.0%. Letting video clips differ from one another therefore brought the simulated data substantially closer to the real scores. The bootstrap reproduced each estimate exactly when every clip received unit weight, but its resampled distributions sat well above the estimates themselves, as often happens with a distance that cannot go below zero and is not a smooth function of the data. For the baseline-and-scale configuration on the score scale, the estimate was 0.2218 while the bootstrap mean was 0.2701, with a basic interval of $[0.1433,0.1992]$ and a percentile interval of $[0.2444,0.3002]$. Since neither interval brackets the estimate in a useful way, @fig-empirical-realism reports the means without intervals, and Appendix C retains the bootstrap means, bias estimates, and both interval constructions as diagnostics.

Taking the two components separately, adding a clip baseline changed the discrepancy by $-0.0418$ and adding a clip scale by $-0.0188$, where negative values favor including the component. Their bootstrap means were $-0.0343$ and $-0.0072$, implying biases of 0.0074 and 0.0116. The basic intervals were $[-0.0577,-0.0423]$ and $[-0.0385,-0.0233]$, and the percentile intervals were $[-0.0413,-0.0258]$ and $[-0.0143,0.0009]$. The clip-scale interval includes zero under one construction and not the other, so we read these paired comparisons descriptively and make no claim of statistical significance. The baseline is the component doing most of the work; the scale helps less and remains optional. Adding the brief activity transition made the discrepancy worse.

The sensitivity analysis that interpolated short gaps produced the same ordering. There the baseline-and-scale configuration had a discrepancy of 0.2511, against 0.3187 for identical clips and 0.2707 for baseline-only, reductions of 21.2% and 7.3%. The baseline-and-scale configuration had the lowest discrepancy of all eight in both representations and both analyses. The individual statistics also show where the resemblance breaks down: in the main analysis the worst agreement was 0.3499 for total variance on the score scale and 0.4423 for the interquartile range of frame-to-frame changes in log-ratio coordinates, the latter rising to 0.4639 after interpolation. Simulated series are therefore still too smooth or too rough from frame to frame in ways the current configuration does not capture, and Appendix C reports every configuration and every statistic. One further caveat bounds all of this: the same test folds were used both to compare the eight configurations and to pick the best one, so the comparison is exploratory and does not account for the uncertainty in that choice. An unbiased assessment would need a new dataset or an outer validation split. Within that limit, the results support the baseline-and-scale configuration as a reasonable starting point for this kind of score series while leaving clear targets for later work. They say nothing about whether the scoring model or its emotion labels are valid.

@fig-lomm-mafw-realism-example shows what this resemblance looks like in a single case. We fixed the 49-frame MAFW clip from @fig-mafwvideo and generated 100 realizations with the baseline-and-scale configuration. The one displayed is the closest of the 100, chosen to minimize the equally weighted mean of the root mean squared error in the scores and in their frame-to-frame changes, each standardized by the corresponding scale in the real data, across all 11 emotions. Its score RMSE was 0.105 and its first-difference RMSE was 0.083.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lomm-mafw-realism-example
#| fig-cap: "Real MAFW classifier scores compared with the closest of 100 LOMM realizations generated for the same 49-frame clip, using the baseline-and-scale configuration. The realization shown minimized the equally weighted mean of the root mean squared error in the scores and in their frame-to-frame changes, each standardized by the corresponding scale in the real data, across all 11 emotions. Thick lines show seven-frame moving averages for the four emotions with the highest mean real scores; faint lines show the unsmoothed scores and the remaining emotions. Because this realization was selected after the fact, it illustrates the best resemblance attainable rather than typical agreement; @fig-empirical-realism carries the aggregate evidence."
#| fig-alt: "Two aligned line plots comparing 49 frames of real MAFW scores with the closest of 100 simulated realizations, both highlighting helplessness, fear, disgust, and sadness."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

realism_example_path <- file.path("figures", "lomm_mafw_closest_timeseries.pdf")
if (!file.exists(realism_example_path)) {
  realism_example_path <- file.path(
    "paper", "figures", "lomm_mafw_closest_timeseries.pdf"
  )
}
knitr::include_graphics(realism_example_path)
```

The selected realization matches the real series in the general size of its scores, in how much they move across several frames, and in the way higher- and lower-scoring emotions vary together. Its peaks do not fall on the same frames, and they should not: LOMM generates new random realizations rather than reconstructing a particular video. Because this series was picked after the fact as the closest of 100, @fig-lomm-mafw-realism-example shows a best case rather than typical agreement; the five-fold results above are the aggregate evidence.

## Study 2 Results: Recovery of the Number of Dimensions

@tbl-method-overall reports the Louvain results for the main $T=100$ benchmark. Recall that worst-case accuracy requires both a usable fit and the correct number of dimensions, so it charges a method for every failure and timeout. Static EGA and the oracle appear alongside the three methods that use the time ordering.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-method-overall
#| tbl-cap: "Louvain results for the main benchmark, with 100 observations per video clip. Each simulated dataset is one independent observation. Usability and worst-case accuracy use all datasets; accuracy conditional on usability uses only the fits that succeeded. Parentheses contain Monte Carlo standard errors."
#| results: asis

method_table_path <- file.path("tables", "table1_method_overall.csv")
if (!file.exists(method_table_path)) {
  method_table_path <- file.path("paper", "tables", "table1_method_overall.csv")
}
method_long <- readr::read_csv(method_table_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(time_points == 100L, community_algorithm == "louvain")
method_counts <- method_long |>
  dplyr::distinct(
    method_id, method_label, n_structure_fits, n_usable_fits,
    n_usable_correct_dimension
  )
method_probabilities <- method_long |>
  dplyr::select(method_id, estimand_id, estimate, monte_carlo_se) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = estimand_id,
    values_from = c(estimate, monte_carlo_se)
  )
method_table_display <- dplyr::left_join(
  method_counts, method_probabilities, by = "method_id"
) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Method = method_label,
    Fits = n_structure_fits,
    Usable = n_usable_fits,
    `Usable and correct` = n_usable_correct_dimension,
    `$P(\\mathrm{usable})$` = sprintf(
      "%.3f (%.4f)", estimate_p_usable, monte_carlo_se_p_usable
    ),
    `$P(\\mathrm{correct}\\mid\\mathrm{usable})$` = sprintf(
      "%.3f (%.4f)",
      estimate_p_correct_given_usable,
      monte_carlo_se_p_correct_given_usable
    ),
    `$P(\\mathrm{usable\\ and\\ correct})$` = sprintf(
      "%.3f (%.4f)",
      estimate_p_usable_and_correct,
      monte_carlo_se_p_usable_and_correct
    )
  )
cat("\\begingroup\\tiny\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  method_table_display,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

All 21,600 DynEGA fits were usable, and 93.9% returned the correct number of dimensions. Static EGA reached 88.4% worst-case accuracy, which shows that a great deal of the structure was already visible in the score levels without using the time ordering at all. GraphicalVAR produced usable fits for 94.1% of datasets and 77.7% worst-case accuracy. GIMME was accurate when it worked, getting the number of dimensions right in 78.3% of its usable fits, but it produced a usable fit only 22.4% of the time, which brings its worst-case accuracy down to 17.6%. The oracle recovered every grouping, confirming that the shared machinery was not itself a source of error.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dimension-recovery
#| fig-cap: "Worst-case accuracy under Louvain across the six scenario families, with 25 or 100 observations per video clip. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals resampling whole datasets. Condition codes are defined in @tbl-scenario-families."
#| fig-alt: "Interval plot of the probability of recovering the correct number of dimensions, by method and simulation scenario."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_5_path <- file.path("figures", "figure5_dimension_recovery.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_5_path)) {
  figure_5_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "figure5_dimension_recovery.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_5_path)
```

@fig-dimension-recovery shows that accuracy varied both by scenario and by the length of the time series. DynEGA was the strongest method in most conditions. Static EGA's high overall accuracy again reflects how much structure was available in the score levels alone when every video clip shared one measurement model; the targeted departures below, particularly independent starting states and between-clip variability, separate the two methods more clearly. GraphicalVAR struggled when expression was weak or measurement was poor. GIMME's low numbers are driven almost entirely by fits that never returned a usable result.

DynEGA also completed the broad grid of 518,400 datasets. Using its own grouping rule, it recovered the correct number of dimensions in 93.7% of datasets and assigned individual indicators to the right dimension 95.2% of the time. Accuracy generally improved with stronger loadings and smaller residual variance, as expected. The $T=300$ conditions also changed the interval between observations, so the difference from $T=100$ reflects the whole design rather than length alone. A separate diagnostic run on the generator characterized the two growing-trajectory families in representative conditions ($N=50$, $k=4$, loading 0.60, residual SD 0.25; 25 replications). The median largest absolute latent value ranged from 55.9 to 105.2 at $T=100$ and from 329.4 to 1,201.6 at $T=300$, and the final tenth of each series accounted for between 0.316 and 0.517 of the total latent energy, with no infinite or missing values. Late-record amplitude can therefore dominate the covariance in those conditions, which is why we treat them as stress tests (Appendix F).

Leiden and Walktrap gave almost the same accuracy as Louvain. The largest spread among the three algorithms was 0.0059 at $T=100$ and 0.0033 at $T=25$, and the targeted departures were similarly stable, with a largest spread of 0.045 for DynEGA on bounded scores and no change in the overall pattern. Appendix G reports these comparisons.

Appendix D reports how well each method recovered the grouping and the trajectories among its usable fits, using ARI, assignment accuracy, trajectory correlation, and NRMSE. Those numbers describe what a method achieves when it works and should be read alongside, not instead of, the worst-case accuracy in @tbl-method-overall.

## Robustness and Sensitivity Analyses

The remaining analyses answer the third question, which concerns how far these results survive departures from ideal conditions. Shortening the time series to $T=25$ gave worst-case accuracy of 0.863 for DynEGA, 0.913 for static EGA, 0.770 for GraphicalVAR, 0 for GIMME, and 1.000 for the oracle. Compared with $T=100$, shorter series cost DynEGA a little, left GraphicalVAR roughly where it was, and made GIMME entirely infeasible. Static EGA actually did somewhat better on the shorter series.

```{r}
#| label: fig-factor-effects
#| fig-cap: "Paired change in worst-case accuracy under each targeted departure, relative to the ideal condition. DynEGA, static EGA, and GraphicalVAR appear throughout; the oracle appears only for the continuous-indicator departures, and GIMME was not fitted here. The oracle is omitted for bounded scores and log-ratio coordinates because it receives the true structure directly and never sees the transformed data. Negative values mean worse accuracy. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals resampling whole datasets."
#| fig-alt: "Interval plot of paired changes in accuracy under departures in starting states, activity transitions, loadings, residuals, inputs, and bounded scores."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_6_path <- file.path("figures", "figure6_factor_effects.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_6_path)) {
  figure_6_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "figure6_factor_effects.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_6_path)
```

Independent starting states were by far the most consequential departure. Accuracy fell from 0.993 to 0.838 for DynEGA, from 0.912 to 0.525 for static EGA, and from 0.683 to 0.253 for GraphicalVAR, while the oracle stayed at 1.000. Giving every dimension the same starting state had therefore been making the main benchmark easier than it looks, a point we return to in the Discussion and that qualifies the population argument in Appendix B. Replacing abrupt switches with five-observation gradual transitions changed almost nothing in the conditions we tested: DynEGA stayed at 0.993, static EGA at 0.912, and GraphicalVAR moved from 0.683 to 0.685. Cross-loadings and correlated inputs across dimensions also produced small changes. Correlated residuals within a dimension actually helped GraphicalVAR and static EGA here, which makes sense: unlike the other two departures it adds no association between dimensions and so reinforces the very grouping the methods are looking for. These are one-at-a-time changes and should not be read as a general ranking of which conditions are hardest.

Bounding the scores changed the question being asked and sharply reduced accuracy on the original channels. DynEGA recovered the correct number of dimensions in 0.333 of the log-ratio datasets and 0.233 of the bounded-score datasets; the corresponding figures were 0.333 and 0.167 for static EGA, and 0.087 and 0.002 for GraphicalVAR. The oracle is omitted here because it receives the true structure directly and never sees the transformed data, so its unchanged result would tell us only that the grouping step still works, not whether constraining scores to sum to one preserves the structure among the original channels. It does not, and these results are the reason Study 1 and Study 2 have to stay separate.

A final analysis added between-clip differences in baseline and scale to selected stable $T=100$ conditions, drawing the baselines within the space spanned by the loadings. It crossed scenarios A--D, $m\in\{2,3\}$, and 10 paired replications, giving 80 paired datasets, each with $N=100$, $k=4$, a loading of 0.60, a residual standard deviation of 0.25, and independent stationary starts; GraphicalVAR and GIMME had fitting limits of 300 and 600 seconds. DynEGA's worst-case accuracy was 0.750 with between-clip differences and 0.775 without, a paired difference of $-0.025$ with a 95% percentile interval of $[-0.100,0.050]$. Static EGA rose from 0.275 to 1.000, because a baseline lying in the loading space adds strong between-clip signal pointing at exactly the right grouping, and static EGA is well placed to use it. GraphicalVAR stayed at 0.0375 and GIMME at 0.400 under both, and the oracle stayed at 1.000. GraphicalVAR's figure rests on three correct fits out of 80 deliberately chosen datasets and is not comparable with its 0.777 across the main benchmark. This was a focused compatibility check rather than a test of equivalence: DynEGA's interval still permits a loss as large as 0.10, every three-dimensional GIMME fit timed out, and GraphicalVAR's unchanged accuracy came with modest declines in ARI and assignment accuracy.

## Computational Feasibility

@fig-runtime-feasibility summarizes how long successful fits took. Counts refer to unique fitted structures, before any structure is reused for a second community-detection algorithm.

```{r}
#| label: fig-runtime-feasibility
#| fig-cap: "Runtime of successful fits in the main benchmark. Points show medians and intervals show interquartile ranges on a log10 scale. Counts use unique fitted structures."
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale interval plot of runtimes for successful fits, by method and time-series length."
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: "0.98\\linewidth"
#| fig-pos: "H"

figure_7_path <- file.path("figures", "figure7_runtime_feasibility.pdf")
if (!file.exists(figure_7_path)) {
  figure_7_path <- file.path("paper", "figures", "figure7_runtime_feasibility.pdf")
}
knitr::include_graphics(figure_7_path)
```

Median runtime for a successful fit was 3.69 s for DynEGA, 85.41 s for GraphicalVAR, and 518.16 s for GIMME, a difference of more than two orders of magnitude between the fastest and slowest. GraphicalVAR completed 20,329 of 21,600 fits and timed out on 1,271. GIMME completed 4,846, timed out on 14,477, and returned errors after estimation for a further 2,277. DynEGA completed every fit in both the main benchmark and the broad grid. These figures describe the specific implementations on this machine and are not a general ranking of how fast these families of methods are. Appendix E gives the full accounting of successes, timeouts, and errors.

# Discussion

LOMM addresses a problem that is becoming common in behavioral research. A classifier will happily produce a dense stream of scores from any video, and a dynamic method will happily return a network or a set of dimensions from that stream, but nothing in the data tells us whether those dimensions were there to be found. LOMM makes that question answerable by separating the latent dynamics, the pattern of expression over time, and the measurement model that produces observed scores, so that each can be changed while the others are held fixed. That separation is the paper's central contribution, because it lets a result be traced back to the part of the generating process responsible for it.

The two studies serve complementary purposes and neither substitutes for the other. Letting video clips differ in baseline and scale brought the simulated scores substantially closer to the real MAFW scores on the summary statistics we chose. That finding is local to one dataset, one set of prompts, and one scoring model, and because the same test folds were used both to compare configurations and to select the best one, it is exploratory rather than an unbiased external validation. It establishes resemblance on chosen statistics; it does not establish that the emotion labels are valid or that LOMM describes how emotional expression actually works. The clip baseline was the component that mattered; the clip scale helped less and remains optional. Reporting all eight configurations in @fig-empirical-realism keeps that choice visible.

Study 2 then supplied a structure known in advance. DynEGA had the highest worst-case accuracy of the methods that estimate from data and was the only one that could complete the broad grid. Static EGA also performed well, which shows that a good deal of the structure was recoverable from score levels alone, without using the time ordering. The two methods came apart under the departures. DynEGA barely changed when video clips were allowed to differ in baseline and scale, whereas static EGA improved sharply, because those differences lie in exactly the space it is looking at. Both lost accuracy under independent starting states. GraphicalVAR often recovered the right number of dimensions when it produced a usable fit, but it was more sensitive to conditions and far more expensive to run. GIMME was usually right when it worked and usually did not work. All of this describes the specific implementations and network conversions we used.

The independent-starting-state result deserves particular emphasis, because it qualifies the main benchmark. Starting every dimension from the same state creates a transient that all dimensions share, which is structure that has nothing to do with the factor model but is nonetheless recoverable. Removing it reduced accuracy for DynEGA, static EGA, and GraphicalVAR alike. Initialization is therefore not an incidental implementation detail but part of the data-generating design, and simulation studies that hold it fixed may be reporting easier problems than they intend. By contrast, smoothing the activity transitions changed little. That comparison concerns the accuracy rate only; it does not separate how much of the derivative signal comes from the oscillator, from the transition, and from measurement error.

Appendix B offers a more general insight into methods that work through networks. Under an idealized model with equal loadings and equal error variances, both the derivative-based and the lagged-residual network preserve the true grouping, and both convert a signal-to-noise ratio into the strength of a within-dimension edge. Crucially, their partial correlations share the same upper bound of $1/(k-1)$. That bound holds regardless of which network is used, so building a network from derivatives carries no automatic advantage at the population level. Whatever differences we observe must come from the signal-to-noise ratio each method achieves, from the length of the time series, from regularization, from how the network is constructed, and from whether the method runs at all. The bound is a mathematical result, not an estimate of why the methods differed in our data. Its wider lesson is that adding common signal cannot strengthen a partial correlation without limit when many indicators are conditioning on one another.

Two details keep that argument aligned with what we actually ran. GraphicalVAR centers within each clip, which slightly reduces residual variance and introduces a small negative covariance between adjacent errors, of order $1/T$; Appendix B carries those terms through, and they change the signal-to-noise ratio without changing the structure of the result. For GIMME, the network we evaluate is built from standardized residual covariances after fitting, which is neither a residual-correlation nor a directed-path network.

The bounded-score results mark a firm boundary on what we can claim. Constraining scores to sum to one changes the associations among the original channels, and neither the scores nor their log-ratio coordinates preserved the result obtained with continuous indicators. A study of recovery from bounded scores would need its own definition of the truth, such as a grouping specified directly in log-ratio coordinates with a fixed basis. Study 1 shows that the generator resembles real scores on selected features; Study 2 shows that the methods recover a known structure from continuous indicators. Neither statement licenses the other.

Several limitations follow from the design. The latent dimensions are uncoupled, and allowing them to drive one another could change both the population argument and the ranking of methods. The growing-trajectory scenarios produce very large amplitudes late in the series and are stress tests rather than plausible affective regimes. The $T=300$ conditions change both the number of observations and the interval between them, so they do not isolate length. GIMME's residual-covariance conversion was built for this comparison and does not represent how the method is normally used. Finally, the real clips are short and come from a single controlled-access dataset scored by a single zero-shot pipeline.

For applied methods work, LOMM suggests a practical order of operations. Decide what the measurement actually is, calibrate only the observable features that matter for the application at hand, specify a truth appropriate to that measurement, and only then evaluate what methods recover and whether they run. Working in that order makes it harder for a classifier's output to acquire substantive meaning simply because a dynamic method returned something interpretable. The present results support LOMM as an environment for that kind of validation, and they point toward extensions with other scoring systems and datasets, coupled rather than independent dimensions, and truth targets defined directly for bounded scores.

# Appendix A: Complete Specification of LOMM

This appendix states LOMM in full. The main text gives the three equations a reader needs to follow the studies; everything omitted there appears here, in the same order as the corresponding main-text material. Nothing in this appendix changes any result. It is intended for readers who want to reimplement the generator or check the claims about what it can and cannot identify.

## A.1 The Latent Transition

Equation 1 of the main text moves each dimension forward one observation interval. Its two components are

$$
\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)=\exp(\mathbf{A}_f\Delta),
\qquad
\mathbf{A}_f=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
\eta_f & \zeta_f
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)=\int_0^{\Delta}\exp(\mathbf{A}_f u)\mathbf{b}\,du,
\quad
\mathbf{b}=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

For the nonzero position-feedback values used in the simulation grids, the input map has the equivalent exact form

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)
=\mathbf{A}_f^{-1}\{\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)-\mathbf{I}_2\}\mathbf{b}.
$$

The integral definition remains valid when $\mathbf{A}_f$ is singular, including $\eta_f=0$. If a root-based closed form is used numerically, a separate repeated-root branch is required when $\zeta_f^2+4\eta_f$ is close to zero.

The state components $x_{if,n}$ and $v_{if,n}$ are the level and its rate of change at $t_n$; $\eta_f$ is position feedback, $\zeta_f$ is velocity feedback, and $\sigma_{qf}$ is the standard deviation of the acceleration input. On the interval $[t_n,t_{n+1})$ the underlying continuous-time model is $\ddot{x}_{if}(t)=\eta_f x_{if}(t)+\zeta_f\dot{x}_{if}(t)+q_{if,n}$ with $q_{if,n}$ held constant, so $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)$ propagates the deterministic state and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)$ loads the input. The inputs are independent across videos, dimensions, and transitions, and independent of initial states, activity schedules, and measurement errors. They are zero-order-hold acceleration inputs rather than increments of a continuous-time white-noise diffusion. The covariance added in one transition is $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)\sigma_{qf}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)^\top$.

## A.2 Dynamic Regimes and Finite-Horizon Amplification

The characteristic roots for dimension $f$ are

$$
r_{f,\pm}=\frac{\zeta_f\pm\sqrt{\zeta_f^2+4\eta_f}}{2}.
$$

Continuous-time asymptotic stability requires $\eta_f<0$ and $\zeta_f<0$, and the roots are oscillatory when $\zeta_f^2+4\eta_f<0$. The exact discrete transition is asymptotically stable when

$$
\rho\{\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)\}
=\exp\!\left[\Delta\max\{\operatorname{Re}(r_{f,+}),\operatorname{Re}(r_{f,-})\}\right]<1.
$$

Negative $\eta_f$ supplies restoring acceleration and negative $\zeta_f$ attenuates velocity, whereas positive $\zeta_f$ produces amplification. How much amplification actually appears depends on the observed horizon. For $T$ observations, $H=(T-1)\Delta$. Let $\alpha(\mathbf{A}_f)=\max\{\operatorname{Re}(r_{f,+}),\operatorname{Re}(r_{f,-})\}$. The quantity

$$
g_f(H)=\exp\{H\alpha(\mathbf{A}_f)\}
$$

is a modal exponential-rate factor over that horizon. It does not by itself measure nonnormal transient amplification or the polynomial factor that can occur at a defective repeated root. A norm-based finite-horizon state-amplification diagnostic is

$$
G_f^{\max}(H)
=
\sup_{0\leq u\leq H}\|\exp(\mathbf{A}_fu)\|_2,
$$

and the corresponding level-only diagnostic is

$$
G_{x,f}^{\max}(H)
=
\sup_{0\leq u\leq H}
\left\|
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}
\exp(\mathbf{A}_fu)
\right\|_2.
$$

The Euclidean matrix norm is coordinate-dependent. Because the state combines a level and a rate of change, whose components have different units, this diagnostic is conditional on the chosen state coordinates and should be interpreted only after fixing a nondimensionalization or an explicit weighted state norm. A coordinate-aware definition is

$$
G_{f,M}^{\max}(H)
=
\sup_{0\leq u\leq H}
\left\|
\mathbf{M}^{1/2}\exp(\mathbf{A}_fu)\mathbf{M}^{-1/2}
\right\|_2,
$$

for a stated positive-definite state metric $\mathbf{M}$; the unweighted $G_f^{\max}(H)$ corresponds to $\mathbf{M}=\mathbf{I}_2$. Reporting the roots and $g_f(H)$ characterizes the modal regime over the observed horizon, but $g_f(H)$ should not be read as total finite-horizon amplification. Reporting the activity schedule separately keeps amplification in the latent dynamics distinct from nonstationarity created by the activity layer.

## A.3 Initial States

The system is uncoupled: $\eta_f$, $\zeta_f$, and $\sigma_{qf}$ may vary by dimension, and off-diagonal dynamic effects are omitted. Study 2's main benchmark initialized every dimension at $x_{if,1}=0.25$ and $v_{if,1}=2$. The sensitivity analysis used independent starting states. For a stable dimension, the stationary covariance $\mathbf P_f$ solves

$$
\mathbf{P}_f=\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)\mathbf{P}_f\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)^\top
+\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)\sigma_{qf}^2\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_f(\Delta)^\top,
$$

whose solution is unique when $\rho\{\boldsymbol{\Phi}_f(\Delta)\}<1$. Drawing $\mathbf{s}_{if,1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{P}_f)$ makes the state process stationary before the activity layer is applied; a time-varying activity envelope still renders $a_{if}(t)x_{if}(t)$ nonstationary. For a dimension with positive velocity feedback, the sensitivity draws $x_{if,1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-0.25,0.25)$ and $v_{if,1}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-2,2)$. These independent starts remove the transient that all dimensions would otherwise share, while leaving the observed horizon unchanged.

## A.4 The Activity Layer at a Transition

Away from a discontinuity in the activity value, the ordinary product rule applies,

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\{a_{if}(t)x_{if}(t)\}
=a_{if}'(t)x_{if}(t)+a_{if}(t)x_{if}'(t).
$$

At an abrupt transition, the derivative of the activity value contains an impulsive component in the distributional sense. Define $D_nx=x_{n+1}-x_n$. The exact discrete identity is

$$
D_n(a_{if}x_{if})
=
a_{if,n+1}D_nx_{if}
+
(D_na_{if})x_{if,n},
$$

where the first term uses the post-transition activity value and the second uses the pre-transition state. The corresponding finite-difference identity is

$$
\frac{\tilde{x}_{if,n+1}-\tilde{x}_{if,n}}{\Delta}
=a_{if,n+1}\frac{x_{if,n+1}-x_{if,n}}{\Delta}
+\frac{a_{if,n+1}-a_{if,n}}{\Delta}x_{if,n}.
$$

The second term is what a derivative-based method sees at a switch even when the oscillator itself has not accelerated, which is the reason for the gradual-transition sensitivity analysis. This convention attaches the new activity value to the post-transition observation, so the activity layer multiplies each completed latent state by the schedule value at the same observation index.

## A.5 The Observation Layer

Let $J$ denote the number of positive score channels, let $d=J-1$, and let $\mathbf V\in\mathbb R^{J\times d}$ be a fixed orthonormal isometric log-ratio (ILR) basis satisfying $\mathbf V^\top\mathbf V=\mathbf I_d$ and $\mathbf V^\top\mathbf 1_J=\mathbf 0$. The basis used here is a normalized Helmert basis constructed in the stated 11-channel order. In Equation 2 of the main text, $\boldsymbol\mu\in\mathbb R^d$ is a fixed center, $\mathbf b_i\in\mathbb R^d$ is the clip baseline, $s_i>0$ is the clip scale, $\kappa>0$ is a global scale, and $\boldsymbol\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ maps the $m$ activity-scaled latent positions into these coordinates. Conditional on the clip-specific terms and $\boldsymbol\Sigma_i$, measurement errors are independent over time and across videos, and independent of latent states, initial states, activity schedules, and acceleration inputs, with $\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{in}\mid\boldsymbol\Sigma_i\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_i)$. Dependence across coordinates follows $\boldsymbol\Sigma_i$. The clip scale multiplies both signal and residual, whereas the baseline is additive.

The three baseline constructions differ only in where $\mathbf b_i$ is allowed to live. Study 1 draws it from a zero-mean Gaussian whose covariance is estimated from training clips in the full coordinate space. Study 2's between-clip-variability analysis instead uses

$$
\mathbf b_i=\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\beta_i,
\qquad E(\boldsymbol\beta_i)=\mathbf 0,
$$

so that between-clip variation stays within the space spanned by the loadings and does not introduce structure outside the factor model. Study 2's main conditions fix $\mathbf b_i=\mathbf 0$ and $s_i=1$, giving the exactly nested homogeneous case

$$
\mathbf u_{in}
=\boldsymbol\mu
+\kappa\left(\boldsymbol\Lambda\tilde{\mathbf x}_{in}
+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{in}\right).
$$

Study 2's continuous indicators are the pre-link quantity

$$
\mathbf z_{in}=\boldsymbol\Lambda_i\tilde{\mathbf x}_{in}+\boldsymbol\varepsilon_{in},
$$

in which each of the $p=mk$ indicators loads on one dimension and has diagonal measurement error.

For bounded output, LOMM maps the coordinates to the open probability simplex. The two log-ratio transformations are

$$
\operatorname{clr}(\mathbf p)
=\log\mathbf p-
J^{-1}\{\mathbf 1_J^\top\log(\mathbf p)\}\mathbf 1_J,
\qquad
\operatorname{ilr}_{\mathbf V}(\mathbf p)
=\mathbf V^\top\operatorname{clr}(\mathbf p),
$$

with the logarithm applied componentwise. Applying Equation 3 of the main text then gives

$$
\operatorname{ilr}_{\mathbf V}(\mathbf p_{in})=\frac{\mathbf u_{in}}{\tau},
\qquad
\operatorname{clr}(\mathbf p_{in})
=\frac{\mathbf V\mathbf u_{in}}{\tau},
$$

the second because $\mathbf V\mathbf u_{in}$ lies in the zero-sum log-ratio subspace. The fixed basis excludes the unidentified common-logit direction and the softmax produces strictly positive rows summing to one, so the scores identify the scaled coordinates $\mathbf u_{in}/\tau$ exactly. A common-logit component remains unobservable, and the unscaled coordinates and $\tau$ are not separately identified without an external scale constraint.

## A.6 Converting Period and Damping to Feedback Parameters

Study 1's search was parameterized by natural period and damping ratio rather than by $\eta_f$ and $\zeta_f$ directly. If $P_f$ is the natural period in observation intervals and $\xi_f$ is the damping ratio, then

$$
\omega_{n,f}=\frac{2\pi}{P_f\Delta},
\qquad
\eta_f=-\omega_{n,f}^2,
\qquad
\zeta_f=-2\xi_f\omega_{n,f},
$$

and the damped angular frequency is $\omega_{d,f}=\omega_{n,f}\sqrt{1-\xi_f^2}$. With $P_f=12$, $\xi_f=0.5$, and $\Delta=1$, these give $\eta_f=-0.2742$ and $\zeta_f=-0.5236$; scaling the inputs to unit stationary position variance gives $\sigma_{qf}=0.5418$.

## A.7 Identifiability

For any nonsingular diagonal matrix $\mathbf{D}$,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{in}
=(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{D}^{-1})(\mathbf{D}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{in}),
$$

so loading magnitude and latent-trajectory scale are not jointly identified without an explicit scale constraint. Activity gain and acceleration-input scale contribute to latent amplitude in the same way. The softmax layer adds invariance to a common location shift and a tradeoff between the temperature and the coordinate scale. Dimension labels are recoverable only up to permutation.

Sampling cadence adds an aliasing restriction. For an underdamped dimension, write

$$
r_{f,\pm}=\frac{\zeta_f}{2}\pm i\omega_f,
\qquad
\omega_f=
\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{-(\zeta_f^2+4\eta_f)}.
$$

At observation times $t_n=(n-1)\Delta$, the frequencies $\omega_f$ and $\omega_f+2\pi q/\Delta$ for integer $q$ generate the same sampled sine and cosine sequences after an appropriate change in initial velocity. Identifying continuous-time oscillator parameters from data therefore requires a cadence-dependent restriction such as

$$
0<\omega_f<\frac{\pi}{\Delta},
$$

together with a specified acceleration-input model and constraints on the latent state basis. Estimating LOMM from data would in total require sign and scale constraints on the dimensions, normalization of the activity schedule, anchoring of either the loading scale or the input scale, a reference-logit or sum-to-zero constraint, a fixed or otherwise identified temperature, and this frequency restriction. Every oscillatory mode used here satisfies the restriction: Study 1 uses $\Delta=1$, giving the most restrictive bound $\pi\approx3.14$ against a largest angular frequency of approximately 0.78, and Study 2 uses $\Delta\in\{0.25,0.4\}$, giving bounds of approximately 12.57 and 7.85 against a largest angular frequency of approximately 1.04. The simulations do not estimate any of these parameters.
