# Appendix B: What Each Method's Network Looks Like in the Population

This appendix works out what the network each method estimates would look like in the population, for Study 2's continuous indicators with every video clip sharing one measurement model. Its purpose is to explain why derivative-based and lagged-residual networks turn out to be more similar than their descriptions suggest. Throughout, a *block* is the set of $k$ indicators loading on a single dimension, so recovering the blocks is the same thing as recovering the assignment of variables to dimensions.

Each method proceeds in four stages: it estimates a structure, converts that structure to a network, applies community detection, and may fail to produce a usable result at all. Estimation and conversion error are treated together, conditional on a usable fit; community detection acts on the network afterward and is not part of the network's error; a failed fit has no network to perturb.

Each analysis can be written as

$$
\widehat{\mathbf S}^{(r)}
\;\xrightarrow{\Pi_r}\;
\widetilde{\mathbf W}^{(r)}
\;\xrightarrow{\mathcal{C}_r}\;
\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{(r)},
$$

where $\widehat{\mathbf S}^{(r)}$ is the fitted method-specific structure and $\Pi_r$ converts it to the graph $\widetilde{\mathbf W}^{(r)}$. The community-detection algorithm $\mathcal{C}_r$ returns the partition $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{(r)}$. Let $U_r$ denote the event that a usable graph exists. Conditional on $U_r=1$,

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf W}^{(r)}
=
\mathbf W_*^{(r)}+\boldsymbol{\Xi}^{(r)},
$$

where $\mathbf W_*^{(r)}$ is the population structural matrix induced by the method's graph construction. The perturbation $\boldsymbol{\Xi}^{(r)}$ includes finite-sample variation, derivative or model estimation, regularization, graph extraction, dependence-induced variance inflation, and systematic deviation from the symmetric target. The community algorithm acts after the graph is formed. When $U_r=0$, there is no estimated graph to perturb.

The derivation has three implications. First, in the ideal case both the DynEGA and the GraphicalVAR population networks preserve the true blocks, provided the relevant cross-block moments are zero. Second, their positive within-block partial-correlation edges share the same ceiling of $1/(k-1)$. How closely a given edge approaches that ceiling depends on the signal-to-noise ratio each method achieves, and the algebra alone does not say which method achieves more. Third, GIMME stands on different footing, because what it recovers also depends on path search, convergence, extraction, averaging, network conversion, and whether it completes at all. Two things this derivation does not cover: Study 1's bounded scores and their log-ratio coordinates, and the between-clip-variability analysis, which adds mean differences across clips that fall outside the zero-mean target assumed here.

```{r}
#| results: asis

assumption_table <- tibble::tribble(
  ~`Result or layer`, ~`Main assumptions`, ~`Sensitivities and interpretation`,
  "Exact block support", "Zero pooled cross-block moments after filtering or projection; one primary loading per indicator; independent measurement errors", "Cross-loadings and correlated acceleration inputs introduce cross-block dependence; within-block residual dependence violates local error independence and can reinforce or distort the block signal",
  "Per-channel filter invariance", "The same linear temporal filter is applied to every indicator, with fixed boundary handling", "Short records, embedding selection, and gate transitions can change finite-sample filter behavior",
  "Within-block edge formula", "Exchangeable loadings and error variances within a block, with positive filtered signal variance", "Loading and variance jitter perturb edge equality while preserving the ideal support target",
  "Connected-component recovery", "The weakest population within-block edge exceeds total graph perturbation conditional on a usable fit", "Regularization, sampling error, and estimation contribute to perturbation; fit failure removes the graph",
  "GIMME recovery decomposition", "A usable contemporaneous graph can be extracted and partitioned", "Convergence, timeout, extraction, symmetrization, and completion are separate analysis stages"
)
cat("\\begingroup\\scriptsize\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{3pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  assumption_table,
  format = "latex",
  caption = "Assumptions behind the Appendix B population results and the corresponding sensitivity analyses.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("p{1.25in}", "p{2.25in}", "p{2.25in}")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

## B.1 Linear Block Target and Pooled Moments

In this appendix, $Y_j$ corresponds to a main-text pre-link score channel $z_j$, $X_f$ to the ungated latent level $x_f$, and $Z_f=a_fX_f$ to the activity-scaled latent level $\tilde{x}_f$. Video indices and loading and variance jitter are omitted to define a symmetric population target.

Consider the population target for the main continuous-indicator benchmark, with $m$ latent dimensions, $k$ observed indicators per dimension, and $p=mk$ observed score channels. Let $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ denote the true indicator blocks. For indicator $j \in B_f$, use the equal-loading, equal-error measurement model

$$
Y_{j,n}=\lambda Z_{f,n}+\varepsilon_{j,n},
\qquad
Z_{f,n}=a_{f,n}X_{f,n},
$$

where $Z_{f,n}$ is the activity-scaled latent oscillator for dimension $f$, $\lambda>0$, and $\varepsilon_{j,n}$ is measurement error with variance $\psi=s_\varepsilon^2$. Measurement errors are independent across indicators and observations in this target, so $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{j,n},\varepsilon_{\ell,h})=0$ whenever $j\neq \ell$ or $n\neq h$.

Let $\mathcal{T}$ denote the rows of the common simulated dataset. Method $r$ retains a subset $\mathcal{R}_r\subseteq\mathcal{T}$. The GLLA derivative series loses rows according to the selected embedding length and boundary rule, whereas the lag-1 projection retains within-video lag pairs. The simulated dataset and physical horizon are common, but the retained rows differ between methods; no common row intersection is imposed. Population moments for method $r$ are taken over $\mathcal{R}_r$. For any quantity $g$,

$$
\langle g\rangle_{\mathcal R_r}
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal R_r|}
\sum_{(i,n)\in\mathcal R_r}
 \mathbb{E}(g_{in}),
$$

and, for any filtered process $U$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R_r}(U)
=
\left\langle
\{U-\langle U\rangle_{\mathcal R_r}\}^{2}
\right\rangle_{\mathcal R_r}.
$$

All variances and covariances in this appendix are time-averaged centered second moments over the rows retained by the method in question. We write this set as $\mathcal{R}$ when the dependence on the method is suppressed. Because the gated and finite-horizon-amplifying processes are nonstationary, different retained windows can yield different $V_{L,f}$, $V_{+,f}$, $V_{-,f}$, $C_f$, and $\theta_{r,f}$ on the same simulated dataset. The choice of retained rows therefore changes the population moments.

Exact block support is imposed through zero pooled cross-block moments over the retained rows. For every pair $f\neq g$ and every method-relevant filter or projection, the corresponding centered cross-block covariance is assumed to be zero. One sufficient set of conditions is that oscillator states are independent across factors at all relevant times and have zero conditional mean at every retained row. Activity schedules must also be deterministic or independent of the states and shocks, and dynamic shocks must be independent across factors. Uncoupled dynamic equations alone do not imply zero pooled cross-block covariance.

Coordinated activity schedules do not create cross-block covariance when factor states have zero conditional means. A shared deterministic initialization, however, can create common mean transients and violate the pooled zero-cross-covariance condition even when the dynamic equations and shocks are uncoupled. The common-start benchmark is therefore a structured departure from the ideal target. The independent zero-mean initialization sensitivity removes this channel.

Activity gating makes $Z_f$ nonstationary by design, which is why the covariances in this appendix are defined as pooled centered moments rather than as stationary second moments. Loading jitter, item-level variance jitter, switching schedules, initialization transients, finite-sample activity imbalance, and estimator behavior are treated as departures or perturbations around this symmetric target.

## B.2 Filtered Series and Two Network Mappings

The derivation uses two population network mappings for a per-channel filtered series. DynEGA estimates local derivatives of every channel; a lag difference is a simple analytic example of the same channelwise operation. GraphicalVAR is treated separately in B.3 because its lag-1 residuals come from a multivariate projection rather than an identical filter applied to each channel.

Let $L$ denote a fixed per-channel linear filter with coefficients $\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_q$, identical boundary handling for every channel, and no window crossing a video boundary. Applying $L$ to the measurement model for $j \in B_f$ gives

$$
(LY_j)_n=\lambda\,(LZ_f)_n+(L\varepsilon_j)_n,
$$

so the filtered series keeps the one-factor block structure. Write

$$
V_{L,f}=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(LZ_f),
\qquad
\psi_L=\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}(L\varepsilon_j)
$$

for the filtered common-signal variance and the filtered noise variance, both centered over the rows retained by the corresponding method. For independent and identically distributed (iid) base measurement error,

$$
\psi_L
=
\psi\sum_{r=0}^{q}\ell_r^2,
$$

and overlapping windows induce the lag covariance

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\{(L\varepsilon_j)_n,(L\varepsilon_j)_{n+h}\}
=
\psi\sum_r\ell_r\ell_{r-h}.
$$

Filtering preserves cross-channel error independence under the ideal error model, so the contemporaneous same-row block covariance remains diagonal plus rank one. Overlapping windows generally make filtered errors serially correlated. This serial dependence does not change the ideal same-row block covariance. It can, however, change the effective sample size, regularization behavior, and sampling variability. Section B.4 therefore treats serial dependence as a source of estimation error rather than incorporating it into the same-row population matrix.

Write $\mathbf J_k=\mathbf{1}_k\mathbf{1}_k^\top$. The within-block covariance matrix of the filtered channels is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{L,f}
=
\lambda^{2}V_{L,f}\,\mathbf J_k+\psi_L \mathbf I_k,
\qquad
\theta_{L,f}=\frac{\lambda^{2}V_{L,f}}{\psi_L},
$$

provided the cross-block filtered moments vanish. Define

$$
C_{L,fg}
=
\left\langle
\{LZ_f-\mu_{L,f}\}
\{LZ_g-\mu_{L,g}\}
\right\rangle_{\mathcal R},
\qquad
\mu_{L,f}
=
\langle LZ_f\rangle_{\mathcal R}.
$$

The block-diagonal covariance and precision formulas in this section require $C_{L,fg}=0$ for all $f\neq g$: exact block support is conditional on these zero pooled cross-block moments after filtering. The filtered signal-to-noise ratio $\theta_{L,f}$ is the only quantity through which the filter enters the population graph.

The filtered series admits two network mappings. The marginal-correlation graph uses correlations directly. For two distinct indicators $j,\ell \in B_f$,

$$
w^{M}_f(L)
=
\left|\operatorname{Cor}(LY_j,LY_\ell)\right|
=
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+\theta_{L,f}}.
$$

The partial-correlation graph conditions each pair on all other retained observed channels. Under exact block diagonality, the other blocks do not change the within-block calculation. Using the Sherman--Morrison identity,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{L,f}^{-1}
=
\psi_L^{-1}
\left[
\mathbf I_k-
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+k\theta_{L,f}}
\mathbf J_k
\right],
$$

and the absolute partial correlation between two indicators in the same block is

$$
w^{P}_f(L)
=
\frac{\theta_{L,f}}{1+(k-1)\theta_{L,f}}.
$$

Because activity gating makes the row distribution time-varying, the inverse of the pooled covariance defines an algebraic partial-correlation graph. It is not interpreted as the conditional-independence graph of one stationary Gaussian process. Under the zero cross-block moment condition, the filtered precision matrix is block-diagonal and cross-block partial correlations are exactly zero. Both graph mappings therefore preserve the generating block support for the per-channel filtered population matrix. For any per-channel filter, the resulting graph has block-clique form,

$$
\mathbf{W}_*
=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
w_1(\mathbf J_k-\mathbf I_k),\ldots,w_m(\mathbf J_k-\mathbf I_k)
\right),
\qquad
w_f\in\{w^{M}_f(L),\,w^{P}_f(L)\}.
$$

The two mappings retain different amounts of within-block signal. For the same signal-to-noise ratio $\theta$,

$$
\frac{w^P(\theta)}{w^M(\theta)}
=
\frac{1+\theta}{1+(k-1)\theta},
$$

so $w^P(\theta)<w^M(\theta)$ whenever $k>2$ and $\theta>0$. As $\theta \to \infty$,

$$
w^P(\theta)\to \frac{1}{k-1},
\qquad
w^M(\theta)\to 1.
$$

The partial-correlation ceiling is a general consequence of this exchangeable block geometry:

$$
\sup_{\theta>0} w^P(\theta)=\frac{1}{k-1}.
$$

Thus, even an arbitrarily strong common-source signal cannot produce a larger within-block partial-correlation edge under the equal-loading, equal-error target. With four indicators per dimension, the ceiling is $1/3$. Both mappings increase with $\theta$. The temporal filter sets $\theta_{L,f}$, and the graph mapping converts that ratio to an edge weight.

@fig-readout-curves compares the marginal- and partial-correlation mappings for the benchmark's four indicators per dimension. The marginal mapping is shown only as a reference before conditioning; neither DynEGA nor GraphicalVAR uses it. The shaded band marks the raw loading-to-error-variance ratio $\lambda^2/s_\varepsilon^2$ in the benchmark rather than a calibrated range of $\theta_{L,f}$. With independent measurement error and a fixed filter, $\theta_{L,f}=(\lambda^2/\psi)V_{L,f}/\sum_r\ell_r^2$. Its position on the $\theta$ axis also depends on $V_{L,f}/\sum_r\ell_r^2$, which varies across scenarios and filters. Strong measurement conditions widen the common-source signal margin, but the partial-correlation edge remains bounded by $1/3$ in the four-indicator target.

The shaded band shows the raw loading-to-error-variance ratios $\lambda^2/s_\varepsilon^2$ in the matched simulation grid for reference. It is not a calibrated range of $\theta_{L,f}$, which also depends on the filtered common-signal variance $V_{L,f}$ and the filter noise gain $\sum_r\ell_r^2$.'

## B.3 Method-Specific Filters and Signal-to-Noise Ratios

The compared methods combine temporal transformations with graph construction. DynEGA estimates generalized local linear approximation (GLLA) derivatives of each score channel over a time-delay embedding window. It then estimates an EBICglasso regularized partial-correlation network from the derivative series. The analysis uses one observation interval for the GLLA spacing parameter; physical time is represented separately by $\Delta=0.4$. With first-order derivatives, a fixed embedding, fixed retained rows, and no zero-variance jitter, conversion to derivatives per unit of physical time applies the same positive scale factor to every channel. The derivative correlation matrix is therefore unchanged. Zero-variance jitter would break this exact invariance if the added noise were not scaled with the derivatives.

### B.3.1 DynEGA and a fixed derivative filter

For a fixed selected GLLA derivative filter with coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\ell}$, let $\mathbf R_{Z,f}$ denote the covariance matrix of the latent values entering the embedding window, centered over the rows retained by the derivative filter. Under iid white measurement error, the population filtered signal-to-noise ratio is

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f}
=
\frac{
\lambda^2\boldsymbol{\ell}^\top \mathbf R_{Z,f}\boldsymbol{\ell}
}{
\psi\,\boldsymbol{\ell}^\top\boldsymbol{\ell}
}.
$$

This population expression is conditional on the chosen embedding and boundary rule. Embedding selection and regularized estimation belong to the finite-sample analysis. DynEGA's population graph is obtained by applying the partial-correlation mapping to this ratio, $w_f^{P}(\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f})$.

A lag-$h$ difference, $D_hY_{j,n}=Y_{j,n+h}-Y_{j,n}$, gives a transparent analytic stand-in for that filter, with

$$
\theta_{f}^{\Delta_h}
=
\frac{
\lambda^2\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal R}
\{Z_{f,n+h}-Z_{f,n}\}
}{
2\psi
},
$$

because independent measurement errors contribute $2\psi$ to the variance of every differenced channel. Both the lag difference and GLLA derivative estimation operate channel by channel. GLLA can reduce white measurement-noise variance by averaging over an embedding window, but it can also attenuate latent change components. Its signal-to-noise ratio is therefore scenario and embedding dependent.

### B.3.2 GraphicalVAR lag-1 projection with finite-clip centering

GraphicalVAR reads partial correlations from the residual covariance of a lag-1 vector autoregression. Its population object is defined here by an unpenalized lag-1 linear projection, $\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{VAR}}$, rather than a per-channel filter. The fitted analysis first standardizes each observed channel across the pooled data and then centers it within each clip before constructing lag pairs. The parameters below are therefore on the globally standardized scale immediately before within-clip centering. Centering changes both the contemporaneous error variance and the lag-1 error covariance.

For a clip with $T$ observations, let

$$
\widetilde\varepsilon_{j,n}
=
\varepsilon_{j,n}-\bar\varepsilon_j,
\qquad
\bar\varepsilon_j=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{h=1}^T\varepsilon_{j,h}.
$$

If the uncentered errors are independent with variance $\psi$, then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde\varepsilon_{j,n})
=\psi\left(1-\frac{1}{T}\right),
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\widetilde\varepsilon_{j,n},
\widetilde\varepsilon_{j,n-1})
=-\frac{\psi}{T}.
$$

No lag pair crosses a clip boundary. Let $\widetilde Z_{f,n}=Z_{f,n}-\bar Z_{f,i}$ denote the within-clip-centered latent signal for the clip containing observation $n$. For one symmetric block, define

$$
V_{-,f}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal R}(\widetilde Z_{f,n-1}^2),
\qquad
V_{+,f}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal R}(\widetilde Z_{f,n}^2),
\qquad
C_f=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal R}(\widetilde Z_{f,n}\widetilde Z_{f,n-1}).
$$

The block moment matrices have the compound-symmetric form

$$
\mathbf S_{--,f}=a_{-,f}\mathbf J_k+b_-\mathbf I_k,
\qquad
\mathbf S_{+-,f}=c_f\mathbf J_k+d\mathbf I_k,
\qquad
\mathbf S_{++,f}=a_{+,f}\mathbf J_k+b_+\mathbf I_k,
$$

where

$$
a_{-,f}=\lambda^2V_{-,f},
\qquad
a_{+,f}=\lambda^2V_{+,f},
\qquad
c_f=\lambda^2C_f.
$$

For equal-length clips and iid errors before centering,

$$
b_-=b_+=\psi\left(1-\frac{1}{T}\right),
\qquad
d=-\frac{\psi}{T}.
$$

The three moment matrices share two eigenspaces: the common direction spanned by $\mathbf 1_k$ and its $(k-1)$-dimensional orthogonal complement. The lag-1 projection residual covariance

$$
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
\mathbf S_{++,f}
-\mathbf S_{+-,f}\mathbf S_{--,f}^{-1}\mathbf S_{-+,f}
$$

therefore has orthogonal and common-direction eigenvalues

$$
r_{\perp,f}
=
b_+-\frac{d^2}{b_-},
\qquad
r_{\parallel,f}
=
b_++ka_{+,f}
-\frac{(d+kc_f)^2}{b_-+ka_{-,f}}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
r_{\perp,f}\mathbf I_k
+
\frac{r_{\parallel,f}-r_{\perp,f}}{k}\mathbf J_k.
$$

When $r_{\parallel,f}>r_{\perp,f}>0$, define

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{\mathrm{centered}}
=
\frac{r_{\parallel,f}-r_{\perp,f}}{kr_{\perp,f}}.
$$

The positive within-block partial-correlation edge then follows the same compression map as B.2:

$$
w_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{P}
=
\frac{
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{\mathrm{centered}}
}{
1+(k-1)\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{\mathrm{centered}}
}.
$$

Finite-clip centering preserves the diagonal-plus-rank-one residual form under the symmetric target, but it changes the signal-to-noise parameter in the partial-correlation mapping. If $r_{\parallel,f}\leq r_{\perp,f}$, the positive-edge graph does not contain the positive within-block signal assumed by the ceiling argument. The residual covariance should be called an innovation covariance only if the lag-1 VAR supplies the relevant innovation process. Oscillator position need not follow a VAR(1), so its projection residuals may remain serially correlated. The result also assumes zero cross-block lag-0 and lag-1 moments. It does not extend directly to cross-loadings, correlated factors, correlated errors, heterogeneous serial measurement error, or lag construction across clip boundaries.

### B.3.3 Uncentered stationary special case and claim boundary

Setting $d=0$ and $b_-=b_+=\psi$ removes within-clip centering and recovers the simpler residual form

$$
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
\psi \mathbf I_k+c_{\mathrm{VAR},f}\mathbf J_k,
\qquad
c_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
\lambda^2V_{+,f}
-
\frac{k\lambda^4C_f^2}{\psi+k\lambda^2V_{-,f}}.
$$

By Cauchy--Schwarz, $C_f^2\leq V_{+,f}V_{-,f}$, and therefore

$$
c_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
\geq
\frac{\lambda^2V_{+,f}\psi}{\psi+k\lambda^2V_{-,f}}
>0.
$$

The associated ratio is $\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}=c_{\mathrm{VAR},f}/\psi$. This uncentered form is a theoretical special case rather than the preprocessing used in the fitted GraphicalVAR analysis. If the latent process is also stationary, with

$$
V_{+,f}=V_{-,f}=V_f,
\qquad
C_f=\rho_{1,f}V_f,
\qquad
\theta_f=\frac{\lambda^2V_f}{\psi},
$$

the uncentered lag-1 residual ratio is

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
=
\theta_f
\left[
1-
\rho_{1,f}^2
\frac{k\theta_f}{1+k\theta_f}
\right],
$$

while a lag-1 difference gives

$$
\theta_{\Delta_1,f}
=
\theta_f(1-\rho_{1,f}).
$$

For $0<\rho_{1,f}<1$, $\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}>\theta_{\Delta_1,f}$. A first difference therefore has lower signal-to-noise than the lag-1 residual in this special case. This result rules out an automatic population advantage for differencing. It does not rank a selected GLLA derivative against the fitted, within-clip-centered GraphicalVAR analysis. As $\rho_{1,f}\to1$,

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}
\to
\frac{\theta_f}{1+k\theta_f},
$$

and, if $\theta_f\to\infty$ in that limit,

$$
w_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{P}
\to
\frac{1}{2k-1},
$$

whereas for fixed $\rho_{1,f}<1$ and $\theta_f\to\infty$ the within-block edge instead approaches the shared $1/(k-1)$ ceiling under the symmetric target.

The population comparison between DynEGA and GraphicalVAR is consequently limited. On the positive branch, both methods produce partial-correlation edges and share the $1/(k-1)$ ceiling under the equal-loading, equal-error target. Both also preserve block support when their relevant cross-block moments are zero. The block algebra does not order $\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{\mathrm{centered}}$. A larger GLLA ratio would require embedding-window noise averaging to outweigh attenuation of the latent derivative signal. That balance must be evaluated from oracle or realized filtered covariances. Section B.4 collects the remaining estimation and graph-conversion differences in a perturbation margin.

## B.4 Shared Perturbation Margin

Let a method's population graph have block-clique form

$$
\mathbf{W}_*^{(r)}
=
\operatorname{blockdiag}
\left(
w_1^{(r)}(\mathbf J_k-\mathbf I_k),\ldots,w_m^{(r)}(\mathbf J_k-\mathbf I_k)
\right),
$$

where edge weights are on the nonnegative scale supplied to community detection and all $m$ blocks share the same size $k$. For DynEGA and GraphicalVAR, $w_f^{(r)}$ equals $w_f^{P}(\theta_{\mathrm{GLLA},f})$ or $w_f^{P}(\theta_{\mathrm{VAR},f}^{\mathrm{centered}})$ from B.3. Each quantity is evaluated on the rows retained by the corresponding method and restricted to the positive branch. Conditional on $U_r=1$, define the perturbation after method-specific graph conversion as

$$
\delta_r
=
\|
\widetilde{\mathbf W}^{(r)}
-
\mathbf W_*^{(r)}
\|_{\max}
=
\max_{j\neq \ell}
\left|
\widetilde{W}^{(r)}_{j\ell}-W^{(r)}_{*,j\ell}
\right|.
$$

For any node $j \in B_f$, the estimated total connection to its true block is at least

$$
(k-1)(w_f^{(r)}-\delta_r),
$$

whereas its estimated total connection to any wrong block is at most

$$
k\delta_r.
$$

Thus each node has stronger total connection to its true block than to any wrong block whenever

$$
(k-1)(w_{\min}^{(r)}-\delta_r)>k\delta_r,
$$

or equivalently

$$
\delta_r
<
\frac{k-1}{2k-1}w_{\min}^{(r)}.
$$

For the matched grid with $k=4$, the sufficient node-level block-preference and threshold-separation condition is

$$
\delta_r < \frac{3}{7}w_{\min}^{(r)},
$$

conditional on a usable graph and the exact block-support population target. This margin does not guarantee that Louvain, Leiden, or Walktrap recover the blocks, because exact recovery depends on the implemented community-detection algorithm. The bound has a narrower consequence. Because $\tfrac{k-1}{2k-1}<\tfrac{1}{2}$, it places every estimated cross-block edge below every estimated within-block edge. Any threshold $\tau\in(\delta_r,\,w_{\min}^{(r)}-\delta_r)$ then deletes all cross-block edges and retains each block as a connected clique. The connected components of the thresholded graph reproduce the generating blocks exactly. Threshold separation alone needs only $\delta_r<w_{\min}^{(r)}/2$.

The margin treats perturbation as symmetric noise on every edge, which makes $\delta_r$ a worst-case envelope. Regularized estimation acts asymmetrically: glasso regularization tends to shrink precision off-diagonal entries toward zero and can remove weak edges, although its effect on each normalized partial correlation need not be monotone. In practice it can reduce $w_{\min}^{(r)}$ while setting weak cross-block edges to zero, which can support block separation.

Under the equal-loading, equal-error symmetric population target, every positive partial-correlation mapping of the diagonal-plus-rank-one block form has the ceiling $1/(k-1)$. DynEGA and GraphicalVAR both have this form under their respective assumptions, so $w_{\min}^{(r)}\leq 1/(k-1)$ for both. With $k=4$, the sufficient perturbation margin approaches at most

$$
\delta_r
<
\frac{3}{7}\cdot\frac{1}{3}
=
\frac{1}{7}
$$

in the high-signal limit of the symmetric target. The comparison therefore depends on two quantities: how closely each filtered or projected ratio brings $w_{\min}^{(r)}$ to the shared ceiling, and the realized perturbation $\delta_r$. An observed recovery ordering does not identify which method has the larger population signal-to-noise ratio because estimation, regularization, graph conversion, and feasibility also differ between methods.

The margin also describes block fragility. Activity gating enters through $V_{L,f}$, the time-averaged centered variance of the filtered activity-scaled process over the retained rows. A dimension held at background gain therefore contributes a smaller $\theta_{L,f}$ and a weaker within-block edge, all else equal. The quantities $V_{L,f}$, $w_{\min}^{(r)}$, and $\mathbf W_*^{(r)}$ remain conditional on the rows retained by each method. This conditioning is especially important for finite-horizon-amplifying factors because their moments grow across the observation window.

In the single-dominance families, background gains are 0.05--0.08 and active gains are 0.35--1.25 (Appendix F). Under comparable ungated filtered variances and error levels, the background gain is expected to reduce $\theta_{L,f}$. The weakest block is the factor with the smallest scenario-specific $V_{L,f}$ and must be identified from the simulated dataset or a population calculation. In the low-expression family, every dimension remains near background activity. The algebra therefore predicts a smaller population separation margin when the activity schedule weakens the least-active block. The recovery patterns in @fig-dimension-recovery are consistent with this prediction, but the simulation does not estimate $\delta_r$ and cannot identify this mechanism on its own. For GIMME, the activity envelope is one of several influences because the resulting graph also depends on path search, convergence, extraction, averaging, graph conversion, and completion.

## B.5 GIMME Graph Conversion

The GIMME comparator has a different mathematical status. Let $\boldsymbol{\Psi}_i^G$ denote the residual covariance matrix extracted for usable clip $i$ after fitting to standardized observed channels, and let $V_u$ be the number of usable clip matrices. Standardized inputs do not force residual variances to equal one, so $\boldsymbol{\Psi}_i^G$ is not a correlation matrix. The averaged matrix is

$$
\bar{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_G
=
\frac{1}{V_u}
\sum_{i:U_i=1}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_i^G,
$$

taken over usable clips only, and the graph supplied to community detection is

$$
\mathbf W_G
=
\left[
\operatorname{offdiag}
\left\{
\frac{\bar{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_G+\bar{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_G^\top}{2}
\right\}
\right]_+.
$$

This procedure produces a positive residual-covariance graph. It is neither a path graph nor a partial-correlation graph. The resulting graph depends on path search, clip-level model selection, convergence, extraction, averaging, and graph conversion. We therefore treat GIMME as an indirect graph-conversion method without a closed-form block edge $w_f^G$.

Worst-case accuracy also charges a method for failing to complete. For any method, let $U$ denote the event that a usable fitted graph exists and $H$ the event that the returned partition is correct, conditional on usability. The worst-case success event is

$$
H^*=U\cap H,
\qquad
P(H^*)
=
P(U)\,P(H\mid U).
$$

Failures and timeouts count as non-hits in $P(H^*)$, but they do not enter $P(H\mid U)$. The primary Louvain results make this decomposition concrete. DynEGA returned a usable network for every simulated dataset in the main benchmark, so its worst-case and conditional correct-dimension rates both equal 0.939. GraphicalVAR was usable for 0.941 of datasets; its conditional correct-dimension rate was 0.826 and its worst-case accuracy was 0.777. GIMME was usable for 0.224 of datasets; its conditional correct-dimension rate was 0.783, but its worst-case accuracy was 0.176. Static EGA was usable for 0.997 of datasets and reached a worst-case accuracy of 0.884. A high conditional rate therefore does not imply high worst-case accuracy when a method often fails to return a network at all.

# Appendix F: Scenario Parameter Values

```{=latex}
\setcounter{table}{0}
\renewcommand{\thetable}{F\arabic{table}}
```

The scenario families use the numeric settings below. The displayed $\sigma_q$ vectors are the per-step shock standard deviations used in the analyses. The 100-observation benchmark uses $\Delta=0.4$. Conditions with 300 observations occur only in the broad DynEGA extension and use $\Delta=0.25$, so these conditions differ in the number of observations, the interval between them, the total time spanned, and discrete shock specification.

Codes A--D use asymptotically stable feedback. Codes E--F use $\eta_f<0$ and $\zeta_f>0$, which produces oscillatory finite-horizon amplification. Their interpretation is restricted to the stated observation horizons. The empirical compositional calibration uses stable negative-$\zeta$ dynamics and is analyzed separately. All oscillatory factors satisfy the cadence restriction $0<\omega_f<\pi/\Delta$ at the observation intervals used here.

```{r}
      Code = code,
      Dimensions = paste0(dimension, "D"),
      eta = fmt_vec(eta[seq_len(dimension)]),
      zeta = fmt_vec(zeta[seq_len(dimension)]),
      `Acceleration-input SD` = fmt_vec(sigma_base[seq_len(dimension)]),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}

))

))
cat("\\endgroup\n\n")
```

```{r}
#| results: asis

print(knitr::kable(
  scenario_dynamic_table,
  format = "latex",
  longtable = TRUE,
  caption = "Dynamic parameters for each scenario family. Acceleration-input SD is the per-step standard deviation $\\sigma_q$ used in each condition.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
```

```{r}
#| results: asis

scenario_vectors <- list(
  A = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  B = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  C = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  D = list(eta = template_eta, zeta = template_zeta),
  E = list(eta = amplification_eta, zeta = amplification_zeta),
  F = list(eta = amplification_eta, zeta = amplification_zeta)
)

stability_rows <- list()
stability_row <- 1L
for (code in names(scenario_vectors)) {
  for (dimension in dimensions) {
    for (factor in seq_len(dimension)) {
      eta_value <- scenario_vectors[[code]]$eta[[factor]]
      zeta_value <- scenario_vectors[[code]]$zeta[[factor]]
      discriminant <- zeta_value^2 + 4 * eta_value
      root_values <- (
        zeta_value + c(-1, 1) * sqrt(as.complex(discriminant))
      ) / 2
      max_real_root <- max(Re(root_values))
      regime <- if (eta_value < 0 && zeta_value < 0) {
        if (discriminant < 0) "Stable oscillatory" else "Stable nonoscillatory"
      } else if (max_real_root > 0) {
        if (discriminant < 0) "Finite-horizon amplifying oscillatory" else "Finite-horizon amplifying nonoscillatory"
      } else {
        "Marginal or mixed"
      }

      stability_rows[[stability_row]] <- data.frame(
        Code = code,
        Dimensions = paste0(dimension, "D"),
        Factor = factor,
        eta = eta_value,
        zeta = zeta_value,
        Discriminant = discriminant,
        `Max Re(root)` = max_real_root,
        `rho(Phi[.4])` = exp(0.4 * max_real_root),
        `rho(Phi[.25])` = exp(0.25 * max_real_root),
        `g(H[100])` = exp((100 - 1) * 0.4 * max_real_root),
        `g(H[300])` = exp((300 - 1) * 0.25 * max_real_root),
        Regime = regime,
        check.names = FALSE
      )
      stability_row <- stability_row + 1L
    }
  }
}
stability_table <- dplyr::bind_rows(stability_rows) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))

cat("\\begingroup\\tiny\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2pt}\n")
print(knitr::kable(
  stability_table,
  format = "latex",
  longtable = TRUE,
  caption = "Deterministic stability diagnostics and modal exponential-rate factors $g(H)=\\exp\\{H\\max\\operatorname{Re}(r)\\}$ for each scenario factor. The $g(H)$ columns describe modal rates over the observed horizon rather than total finite-horizon state amplification. $H[100]=39.6$ and $H[300]=74.75$ under the stated record designs.",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  align = c("c", "c", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "l")
))
cat("\\endgroup\n")
```

Their results were closely aligned in the matched designs (@fig-community-sensitivity) and led to the same interpretation of the targeted departures (@fig-challenge-community-sensitivity).
